topics.title: What is C and the Structure of a C Program

lesson.summary: C is a general-purpose, procedural programming language developed in the early 1970s, and every C program follows a fixed structure starting with preprocessor directives, a main function, and statements inside curly braces.
shortNotes: C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs around 1972 and is the foundation for many modern languages.
Every C program must have exactly one main() function — execution always starts there.
Preprocessor directives like #include <stdio.h> are processed before compilation and bring in library functions.
Statements inside a function are enclosed in curly braces { } and each statement ends with a semicolon.
printf() is used to print output to the screen and is declared in the stdio.h header file.
The return 0; statement at the end of main() tells the operating system the program finished successfully.

detailed.explanation:
C is a general-purpose, procedural programming language created by **Dennis Ritchie** at Bell Labs (AT&T) around **1972**. It was originally developed to write the UNIX operating system. C is called a *middle-level* language because it combines features of high-level languages (easy to read) with low-level access to memory and hardware. Languages like C++, Java, and Python were heavily influenced by C.

Every C program has a **fixed skeleton structure**. At the top you write *preprocessor directives* — lines that start with `#`. The most common one is `#include <stdio.h>`, which tells the compiler to include the Standard Input Output library so you can use functions like `printf` and `scanf`.

After the directives comes the **main function**: `int main()`. This is the entry point — when you run a C program, the computer always starts executing from the first line inside `main`. The body of the function is wrapped in curly braces `{ }`. Inside the body you write your statements, each ending with a **semicolon** `;`.

The statement `printf("Hello, World!\n");` prints text to the screen. The `\n` is an *escape sequence* that moves the cursor to a new line. At the end of `main`, writing `return 0;` signals to the operating system that the program ran without errors. A non-zero return value traditionally means something went wrong.

definitions.meaning: A command starting with # that is handled before actual compilation, e.g., #include <stdio.h> adds the standard I/O library.
The mandatory entry-point function in every C program; execution begins from the first statement inside it.
A file (e.g., stdio.h) that contains declarations of library functions so the compiler knows how to use them.
A single instruction in C that performs an action; every statement ends with a semicolon.
A special two-character code starting with a backslash that represents a non-printable character, e.g., \n for newline.
A program (e.g., GCC) that translates C source code into machine code that the computer can execute.
A statement at the end of main() that returns the value 0 to the operating system, indicating successful execution.

points: C was developed by Dennis Ritchie in 1972 at Bell Labs — this is a very common exam fact.
Every valid C program must contain a main() function; without it the program will not compile or run.
#include <stdio.h> must be written before using printf() or scanf(); forgetting it is a classic beginner error.
Each statement must end with a semicolon (;) — missing semicolons are the most frequent compilation error.
Curly braces { } define the body (block) of a function; every opening brace must have a matching closing brace.
The return type of main() is int; writing int main() is the standard and preferred form in modern C (C99 and later).
printf() is used for output and scanf() is used for input — both live in stdio.h.
C is case-sensitive: Main() and main() are treated as completely different names by the compiler.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: #include <stdio.h> — preprocessor directive that includes the Standard Input Output header file, giving access to printf().
Line 3: int main() — declares the main function with return type int; this is where program execution begins.
Line 4: { — opening curly brace marks the start of the main function body.
Line 6: printf("Hello, World!\n"); — calls the printf function to print the text 'Hello, World!' followed by a newline character (\n).
Line 9: printf("Welcome to C Programming.\n"); — prints a second line of text to the screen.
Line 11: return 0; — returns the integer 0 to the operating system, indicating the program ended successfully.
Line 12: } — closing curly brace marks the end of the main function body.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the semicolon (;) at the end of a statement — this is the single most common compilation error and produces a 'expected ;' error message.
Writing #include<stdio.h> but then misspelling printf as Printf or PRINTF — C is case-sensitive, so only the lowercase version works.
Omitting the return 0; statement or writing return; without a value — while some compilers may accept it, it is bad practice and can cause warnings or undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Who created the C programming language?
questions.explanation: Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs around 1972. Bjarne Stroustrup created C++, James Gosling created Java, and Guido van Rossum created Python.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct entry point of a C program?
questions.explanation: Every C program must have a main() function. The operating system calls main() to begin execution of the program.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of #include <stdio.h> in a C program?
options: It tells the linker to create an executable
It includes the Standard Input Output header so functions like printf() can be used
It allocates memory for the program
questions.explanation: #include <stdio.h> is a preprocessor directive that includes the standard I/O library header, which contains declarations for printf(), scanf(), and other I/O functions.

questions.prompt: What does the escape sequence \n do inside a printf() string?
options: Moves the cursor to a new line
questions.explanation: \n is a newline escape sequence. When printf() encounters \n in a string, it moves the output cursor to the beginning of the next line.

questions.prompt: What will happen if you forget the semicolon at the end of printf("Hello");?
options: The program will compile and run normally
The compiler will produce a syntax error
The program will print an extra blank line
questions.explanation: In C, every statement must end with a semicolon. Missing a semicolon causes a compilation (syntax) error and the program cannot be built.

questions.prompt: What value should main() return to indicate that the program executed successfully?
questions.explanation: By convention, returning 0 from main() tells the operating system that the program completed without errors. Non-zero values indicate errors.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of a preprocessor directive in a C program and give one example.
questions.answer: A preprocessor directive is an instruction (starting with #) that is processed before the actual compilation of the program. It is used to include header files or define constants. For example, #include <stdio.h> includes the Standard Input Output header file, which provides access to functions like printf() and scanf().
questions.explanation: A good answer must mention that directives start with #, are processed before compilation, and give a concrete example like #include <stdio.h>.

questions.prompt: Why is C sometimes called a middle-level programming language?
questions.answer: C is called a middle-level language because it combines features of both high-level and low-level languages. Like a high-level language, it has readable syntax and supports structured programming. Like a low-level language, it allows direct manipulation of memory through pointers and close interaction with hardware.
questions.explanation: The answer should address both sides: readability like a high-level language and direct memory/hardware access like a low-level language.

questions.answer: CProgramming
questions.explanation: There is no space or newline between the two printf() calls and neither string contains \n or a space, so the outputs are concatenated directly to give CProgramming on a single line.

questions.prompt:
Write a complete C program that prints the following two lines exactly:
I am learning C.
C was made in 1972.
questions.explanation: Two printf() calls are needed, one for each line. Each string ends with \n to move to the next line after printing. The #include <stdio.h> directive is required to use printf(), and return 0; signals successful completion.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are going to learn about C programming — one of the most important languages you will ever study.
C is a general-purpose programming language created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972.
It was originally built to write the UNIX operating system, and it is the parent of languages like C plus plus, Java, and Python.
C gives you both readable code and direct control over memory, which is why we call it a middle-level language.
Every C program follows the same fixed structure. Let us build it on the board step by step.
The very first line is a preprocessor directive. We write hash include stdio dot h to bring in the input output library.
Next comes the main function. We write int main with empty parentheses and an opening curly brace.
Inside the braces we write our statements. Here we use printf to print Hello World followed by a newline.
Finally we write return zero and close the brace. Return zero tells the operating system the program finished successfully.
Let us quickly go through what each part does so it is crystal clear.
Hash include stdio dot h is a preprocessor directive. It runs before compilation and loads the I O library.
int main is the entry point. The computer always starts running your program from the first line inside main.
printf prints text to the screen. The backslash n inside the string is an escape sequence that moves to a new line.
Every statement ends with a semicolon. If you forget even one semicolon, the compiler will give you an error.
The number one mistake beginners make is forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement. Let me show you.
This line is missing the semicolon at the end. The compiler will stop and report a syntax error.
This is the correct version with the semicolon in place. Always double-check every statement.
Also remember that C is case-sensitive, so main with a capital M is not the same as main with a small m.
Great work! Let us do a quick recap of everything we covered today.
C was created by Dennis Ritchie in 1972 and influenced almost every popular language that came after it.
Every C program starts with hash include, then int main, then statements inside curly braces, and ends with return zero.
Remember: every statement needs a semicolon, and C is case-sensitive. Keep these two rules in mind and you will avoid most beginner errors.

topics.title: Compiling and Running a C Program

lesson.summary: To run a C program, you must first write the source code, then compile it using a compiler like GCC, and finally execute the output file.
shortNotes: C is a compiled language — source code must be converted to machine code before it can run.
The most common compiler used in India's colleges is GCC (GNU Compiler Collection).
The basic compile command is: gcc filename.c -o outputname
If there are no errors, the compiler produces an executable file you can run.
On Linux/Mac run the program with ./outputname; on Windows use outputname.exe
Compilation errors must be fixed in the source code before a working program is produced.

detailed.explanation:
A C program goes through several steps before it actually runs on your computer. First, you write the **source code** in a text editor or IDE and save it with a `.c` extension (for example, `hello.c`). This file contains human-readable instructions.

Next, you **compile** the source code using a C compiler. The most widely used compiler is **GCC** (GNU Compiler Collection), which is free and available on Linux, Windows (via MinGW), and macOS. The compiler reads your `.c` file, checks it for syntax errors, and converts it into a binary **executable** file that the computer's processor can understand.

The basic GCC command looks like this:
```
gcc hello.c -o hello
```
Here, `gcc` calls the compiler, `hello.c` is your source file, `-o hello` tells the compiler to name the output file `hello`. If you omit `-o`, GCC creates a default file called `a.out` on Linux/Mac.

If the compilation is successful (no errors), you run the executable. On Linux or macOS type `./hello` in the terminal. On Windows, type `hello.exe`. The program then executes and you see the output on the screen.

If the compiler finds **errors**, it prints messages telling you the line number and type of problem. You must go back to your source code, fix the errors, and compile again. This edit-compile-run cycle is the core workflow every C programmer uses.

definitions.meaning: The human-readable C instructions you write and save in a .c file.
A program that translates source code into machine-executable binary code.
GNU Compiler Collection — a free, widely used C compiler available on most operating systems.
The binary output file produced by the compiler that the computer can directly run.
A mistake in the source code (like a missing semicolon) that prevents the compiler from producing an executable.
The text-based interface where you type commands to compile and run your program.

points: The file extension for a C source file is .c (e.g., hello.c).
GCC is the standard compiler used in most Indian universities; learn its basic flags.
The flag -o lets you name your output file; without it the default name is a.out.
Always check the terminal output after compiling — no news is good news (no errors means success).
Warnings are different from errors: the program may still compile but could behave unexpectedly.
Use -Wall flag (gcc hello.c -Wall -o hello) to see all warnings — good habit from day one.
On Windows, the executable is hello.exe; on Linux/Mac it has no extension but is run with ./hello.
The edit-compile-run cycle is fundamental: change code → compile → test → repeat.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: #include <stdio.h> — includes the Standard Input/Output library so we can use printf.
Line 3: int main() — the main function; every C program starts executing from here.
Line 4: printf("Hello, World!\n"); — prints the text to the screen; \n moves the cursor to a new line.
Line 5: return 0; — tells the operating system the program finished successfully.
To compile: gcc hello.c -o hello
To run on Linux/Mac: ./hello
To run on Windows: hello.exe
Expected output: Hello, World!

commonMistakes: Forgetting to save the .c file before compiling — the compiler works on the saved version, not unsaved changes.
Typing the compile command incorrectly (e.g., missing the filename or misspelling gcc) and being confused by 'command not found' errors.
Not adding ./ before the program name on Linux/Mac when running (e.g., typing hello instead of ./hello), which gives a 'command not found' error.

questions.prompt: Which command correctly compiles a file named program.c and names the output file program using GCC?
questions.explanation: gcc -o program program.c is the correct syntax. The -o flag specifies the output filename. Option C would work but creates a.out, not program. Options B and D are not valid commands.

questions.prompt: What is the default output filename when you compile with GCC without using the -o flag on Linux?
questions.explanation: When you do not specify -o, GCC automatically names the executable a.out on Linux and macOS systems.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct way to run an executable named hello on a Linux terminal?
questions.explanation: ./hello is correct on Linux/Mac. The ./ tells the shell to look in the current directory. Just typing hello may fail if the current directory is not in the system PATH.

questions.prompt: What does the GCC flag -Wall do?
options: Compiles all .c files in the folder
questions.explanation: -Wall stands for 'warnings all'. It tells GCC to display all common warning messages, helping you catch potential bugs even when there are no fatal errors.

questions.prompt: What type of file does a C compiler produce as output?
questions.explanation: The compiler converts human-readable source code (.c file) into a binary executable file containing machine code that the processor can run directly.

questions.prompt: If GCC finds a syntax error in your code during compilation, what happens?
options: It compiles anyway and the error is fixed automatically
It prints an error message and does NOT produce an executable
It produces an executable but it runs incorrectly
It opens your source file and fixes it
questions.explanation: When GCC encounters a syntax error it stops compilation, prints an error message with the line number and description, and does not create an executable file. You must fix the code and recompile.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a compilation error and a runtime error in a C program.
questions.answer: A compilation error is a mistake (like a missing semicolon or undeclared variable) that the compiler detects before the program runs; it prevents an executable from being produced. A runtime error occurs after successful compilation, while the program is actually running, such as dividing by zero or accessing invalid memory.
questions.explanation: Understanding the two stages — compile time and run time — helps programmers know when and where to look for different kinds of bugs.

questions.prompt: What is the role of #include <stdio.h> at the top of a C program?
questions.answer: #include <stdio.h> is a preprocessor directive that includes the Standard Input/Output header file. It gives the program access to functions like printf and scanf that handle input and output. Without it, the compiler will not recognize these functions.
questions.explanation: Header files declare functions from standard libraries. Including stdio.h is necessary whenever you use any standard I/O functions in your program.

questions.answer: Score: 15
questions.explanation: 10 + 5 evaluates to 15. The printf statement prints the string 'Score: ' followed by the integer value 15. There is no newline character so nothing extra is printed.

questions.prompt: Write a complete C program that prints your name and your college name on two separate lines. Use printf for each line.
questions.explanation: Each printf call prints one line. The \n at the end of each string moves the cursor to the next line so the two pieces of information appear on separate lines. The actual name and college can be any valid strings.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are going to learn how to compile and run a C program. This is the very first practical skill every C programmer needs.

write.content: Compiling and Running a C Program

steps.say: Computers do not understand the English-like code we write. A compiler is a special program that translates our code into machine language.

write.content: Compiler: translates C code → machine code

steps.say: We write our code in a dot-c file, the compiler reads it, and produces an executable file we can actually run.
Let us write a simple program. Every C program starts with including the standard input output library.
Now we add the main function. Execution of every C program begins from main.
Inside main, we call printf to print Hello World on the screen. The backslash n moves to the next line.
Finally, return zero tells the operating system the program finished successfully. Then we close the curly brace.
Save the file as hello dot c. Now open your terminal and type the GCC command to compile it.
Type g c c, then the filename hello dot c, then dash o hello. The dash o flag sets the name of the output file.
If there are no errors, the compiler silently creates an executable file called hello. No message means success!
If you see an error message, read it carefully. It tells you the line number and what went wrong. Fix it and compile again.

write.content: Error shown → fix code → compile again

steps.say: Once compiled, run the program. On Linux or Mac, type dot slash hello in the terminal.
On Windows, type hello dot exe to run the program.
You should see Hello World printed on the screen. Congratulations, you just ran your first C program!
Let us quickly recap what we covered today. The full process has three simple steps.
Step one: write your code and save it as a dot c file.
Step two: compile using g c c with the dash o flag to name your output.
Step three: run the executable. Use dot slash on Linux and Mac, or just the name on Windows. Keep practising this cycle every day!

lesson.summary: Variables are named memory locations that store data, and data types tell the compiler what kind of data will be stored in those locations.
shortNotes: A variable is a named storage location in memory that holds a value which can change during program execution.
Every variable in C must be declared with a data type before it can be used.
Common basic data types in C: int (integer), float (decimal), double (larger decimal), char (single character).
The size of data types can vary by system; use sizeof() operator to check the exact size in bytes.
Variable names must start with a letter or underscore and cannot be a C keyword (e.g., int, return).
Initializing a variable means assigning a value at the time of declaration, e.g., int age = 20;

detailed.explanation:
In C programming, a **variable** is a named location in the computer's memory where you can store a value. Think of it like a labelled box — the label is the variable name, and whatever you put inside is the value. You can change the value inside the box at any time during program execution, which is why it is called a 'variable'.

Before you can use a variable in C, you must **declare** it. A declaration tells the compiler two things: the name of the variable and the **data type** — that is, what kind of data it will hold. The syntax is simple: `int age;` declares a variable called `age` that will store whole numbers.

C provides several built-in **primitive data types**. `int` stores whole numbers (e.g., 5, -3, 100). `float` stores decimal numbers with about 6–7 digits of precision (e.g., 3.14). `double` stores decimal numbers with about 15–16 digits of precision and uses more memory. `char` stores a single character (e.g., 'A', 'z', '5') and is stored internally as a small integer using ASCII values.

You can **initialize** a variable when you declare it: `int marks = 95;`. If you declare a variable without initializing it, it may hold a garbage (random) value — this is a very common source of bugs for beginners. Always initialize variables before using them.

The `sizeof()` operator is very useful — it returns the number of bytes a data type or variable occupies in memory. For example, `sizeof(int)` typically returns 4 on most modern systems. Knowing sizes helps you understand memory usage and avoid overflow errors.

definitions.meaning: A named memory location that stores a value which can be read and modified during program execution.
A classification that tells the compiler what kind of data a variable will hold and how much memory to allocate for it.
A statement that introduces a variable to the compiler by specifying its data type and name, e.g., int x;
Assigning an initial value to a variable at the time of its declaration, e.g., int x = 10;
A data type used to store whole numbers (integers), typically occupying 4 bytes on modern systems.
A data type used to store single-precision decimal (floating-point) numbers, typically 4 bytes.
A data type used to store double-precision decimal numbers with greater accuracy than float, typically 8 bytes.
A data type used to store a single character, occupying 1 byte and using ASCII encoding internally.
A built-in C operator that returns the size (in bytes) of a data type or variable at compile time.

points: Always declare a variable before using it — C does not allow undeclared variables.
Variable names are case-sensitive: `Age`, `age`, and `AGE` are three different variables.
A variable name cannot start with a digit; it must start with a letter (a-z, A-Z) or an underscore (_).
C keywords like `int`, `return`, `if`, `while` cannot be used as variable names.
Uninitialized local variables contain garbage values — always initialize before use to avoid bugs.
Use `%d` format specifier for `int`, `%f` for `float`, `%lf` for `double`, and `%c` for `char` in printf/scanf.
The `double` type is preferred over `float` for scientific calculations because of its higher precision.
Exam tip: sizeof(char) = 1, sizeof(int) = 4, sizeof(float) = 4, sizeof(double) = 8 on most 32/64-bit systems.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: Include stdio.h for input/output functions like printf.
Line 3: main() is the entry point of every C program.
Line 5: Declare and initialize an integer variable 'age' with value 20.
Line 6: Declare and initialize a float variable 'cgpa' with a decimal value.
Line 7: Declare and initialize a double variable 'distance' with a high-precision decimal.
Line 8: Declare and initialize a char variable 'grade' with the character A (use single quotes for char).
Lines 11-14: Print each variable using its matching format specifier (%d for int, %f for float, %lf for double, %c for char). %.2f means print float with 2 decimal places.
Lines 17-21: Use sizeof() with %zu format specifier to print the memory size of each data type in bytes.
Line 24: Reassign a new value (21) to the variable 'age' — this shows variables can change.
Line 25: Print the updated value of age.
Line 27: return 0 signals successful program termination to the operating system.

commonMistakes: Using a variable without declaring it first — C requires every variable to be declared with a data type before use; forgetting this causes a compilation error.
Using the wrong format specifier in printf/scanf — for example, using %f to print an int or %d to print a float gives incorrect output or undefined behavior.
Not initializing a variable before using it — local variables in C are not automatically set to zero; they contain garbage values, which can cause unpredictable results in calculations.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a valid variable name in C?
questions.explanation: '_total' is valid because variable names can start with an underscore. '2marks' starts with a digit (invalid), 'int' is a reserved keyword (invalid), and 'my-score' contains a hyphen which is not allowed.

questions.prompt: What is the correct format specifier for printing a float variable using printf()?
questions.explanation: %f is the correct format specifier for float. %d is for int, %c is for char, and %lf is used for double.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does a char data type typically occupy in C?
questions.explanation: A char data type always occupies exactly 1 byte (8 bits) in C. This is guaranteed by the C standard (sizeof(char) == 1 always).

questions.prompt: Which data type should you use to store the value 3.14159265358979 with maximum precision in C?
questions.explanation: double provides about 15-16 decimal digits of precision, which is much better than float's 6-7 digits. For values like pi that require high precision, double is the correct choice.

questions.prompt: What will happen if you use a local variable in C without initializing it?
options: The compiler will automatically set it to 0
It will contain a garbage (unpredictable) value
questions.explanation: In C, local variables that are declared but not initialized contain whatever value happens to be at that memory address — called a garbage value. The compiler does not automatically initialize local variables to zero.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly declares AND initializes an integer variable named 'score' with value 85?
questions.explanation: The correct C syntax is: data_type variable_name = value; — so 'int score = 85;' is correct. 'integer' is not a valid C keyword; the correct keyword is 'int'.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between float and double data types in C?
questions.answer: Both float and double are used to store decimal (floating-point) numbers in C. The key difference is precision and size: float uses 4 bytes and provides about 6-7 significant decimal digits of precision, while double uses 8 bytes and provides about 15-16 significant decimal digits. double is preferred when higher accuracy is needed.
questions.explanation: Students should understand that the core distinction is precision (number of accurate decimal digits) and memory size. double is called 'double precision' because it has roughly double the precision of float.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to always initialize a variable in C before using it in a calculation?
questions.answer: Uninitialized local variables in C contain garbage values — whatever random data happens to be at that memory location. If you use such a variable in a calculation, the result will be unpredictable and incorrect. Always initializing variables ensures your program produces correct and consistent results.
questions.explanation: Unlike some other languages, C does not automatically zero-initialize local variables. This is a deliberate design choice for performance, but it puts the responsibility on the programmer to initialize variables before use.
The variable x is 10. y is 2.5 but is cast to int, which truncates it to 2 (int cast drops the decimal part). So x + (int)y = 10 + 2 = 12. The format specifier %d prints it as an integer: 12.

questions.prompt: Write a complete C program that declares variables to store a student's name initial (char), age (int), and percentage marks (float). Initialize them with any valid sample values and print all three values with appropriate labels using printf().
questions.explanation: We declare three variables with appropriate types: char for the initial (single character, stored in single quotes), int for age (whole number), and float for percentage (decimal number). Each is initialized with a sample value. In printf(), we use %c for char, %d for int, and %.2f for float (showing 2 decimal places). The %% in the format string prints a literal percent symbol.

steps.say: Hello everyone! Today we are going to learn about one of the most fundamental building blocks of C programming — variables and data types.

write.content: Variables and Data Types in C

steps.say: Think of a variable as a labelled box in your computer's memory. You give the box a name, and you can put a value inside it.
The value inside the box can change any time during the program — that is exactly why we call it a variable.
In C, before you use any variable, you must declare it. A declaration has two parts — the data type and the variable name.
For example, to store a student's age as a whole number, we write: int age semicolon.
We can also give it a starting value right away — this is called initialization. Here we set age equal to 20.
Always initialize your variables. If you do not, the variable holds a garbage value — random data left over in memory.
Now let us look at the four most common data types you will use in C programming.
int stores whole numbers. float stores decimal numbers. double stores decimal numbers with much higher precision.
And char stores a single character like the letter A, which you write inside single quotes.
Each type tells the compiler exactly how much memory to reserve and how to interpret the stored bits.
The sizes are typically: int and float are 4 bytes each, double is 8 bytes, and char is always 1 byte.
Let us see all of this together in a short C program. We start with the standard include and main function.
Now we declare and initialize one variable of each type — age as int, cgpa as float, and grade as char.
Next we print them. Notice we use percent d for int, percent f for float, and percent c for char.
We close the program with return zero and a closing brace. When we run this, it prints 20, 8.75, and A.
Great work! Let us quickly recap what we learned today about variables and data types.
A variable is a named memory location. You must declare it with a data type before using it.
The four basic types are int, float, double, and char. Each has a specific size and purpose.
Always initialize your variables to avoid garbage values. Use the correct format specifier when printing with printf.
Practice writing small programs with different data types — that is the best way to get comfortable with these concepts. See you in the next lesson!

lesson.summary: Operators and expressions in C are the building blocks that let you perform calculations, compare values, and combine conditions to create meaningful programs.
shortNotes: An operator is a symbol that tells the compiler to perform a specific operation on operands, e.g., +, -, *, /.
An expression is a combination of variables, constants, and operators that evaluates to a single value.
C has several operator categories: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, bitwise, and miscellaneous.
The modulus operator % gives the remainder of integer division, e.g., 10 % 3 = 1.
Operator precedence determines which operator is evaluated first; parentheses can override the default order.
The increment (++) and decrement (--) operators add or subtract 1 from a variable and can be prefix or postfix.

detailed.explanation:
An **operator** is a special symbol used to perform operations on one or more **operands** (values or variables). For example, in the expression `a + b`, the `+` symbol is the operator and `a`, `b` are the operands. An **expression** is any valid combination of operators and operands that produces a value, such as `2 * x + 5`.

C provides several types of operators. **Arithmetic operators** (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) perform math. **Relational operators** (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) compare two values and return 1 (true) or 0 (false). **Logical operators** (`&&`, `||`, `!`) combine or negate conditions. **Assignment operators** (`=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`) store values in variables.

**Operator precedence** controls the order of evaluation. Multiplication and division have higher precedence than addition and subtraction, so `2 + 3 * 4` evaluates as `2 + 12 = 14`, not `20`. Use parentheses to explicitly control the order: `(2 + 3) * 4 = 20`.

The **increment (`++`) and decrement (`--`) operators** are very common in C. `++a` (prefix) increments first and then uses the value, while `a++` (postfix) uses the value first and then increments. For example, if `a = 5`, then `b = ++a` sets `a = 6` and `b = 6`, but `b = a++` sets `b = 5` and then `a = 6`.

The **modulus operator `%`** works only on integers and returns the remainder. It is frequently used to check if a number is odd or even: `n % 2 == 0` means `n` is even. Understanding these operators thoroughly is essential because nearly every C program uses them.

definitions.meaning: A symbol that instructs the compiler to perform a specific operation on operands, e.g., +, -, *, /.
A value or variable on which an operator acts, e.g., in a + b, both a and b are operands.
A combination of variables, constants, and operators that evaluates to a single value, e.g., 2 * x + 5.
The rule that determines which operator in an expression is evaluated first when there are multiple operators.
When two operators have equal precedence, associativity determines whether evaluation goes left-to-right or right-to-left.
Returns the integer remainder after division; works only with integer operands, e.g., 10 % 3 = 1.
Adds 1 to a variable. Prefix (++a) increments before use; postfix (a++) increments after use.
Subtracts 1 from a variable. Prefix (--a) decrements before use; postfix (a--) decrements after use.

formulas.name: Integer Division
formulas.note: Both a and b must be integers; fractional part is discarded.

formulas.name: Modulus
formulas.note: Works only for integer operands; gives the remainder after division.

formulas.name: Compound Assignment
formulas.expression: a += b  is equivalent to  a = a + b
formulas.note: Similarly: -=, *=, /=, %= all work the same way.

points: Always use == for comparison and = for assignment; mixing them up is one of the most common bugs in C.
Integer division truncates the decimal part: 7 / 2 gives 3, not 3.5. Use float/double if you need the decimal.
Operator precedence table (high to low): ++ / -- > * / % > + / - > relational > logical > assignment.
Parentheses always override precedence, so use them freely to make your code clearer and correct.
The modulus operator % cannot be used with float or double operands — it only works with integers.
In postfix a++, the original value is used in the expression first, and the variable is updated after.
Logical AND (&&) returns true only if both operands are true; Logical OR (||) returns true if at least one is true.
Short-circuit evaluation: in &&, if the first condition is false, the second is not checked; in ||, if the first is true, the second is not checked.

topics.title: Input and Output with printf and scanf

lesson.summary: In C programming, printf is used to display output on the screen and scanf is used to read input from the user, both relying on format specifiers to handle different data types.
shortNotes: printf() prints formatted output to the console; it is defined in the stdio.h header file.
scanf() reads formatted input from the keyboard; it also requires stdio.h.
Format specifiers like %d (int), %f (float), and %c (char) tell the functions what type of data to handle.
scanf() requires the address of the variable using the & (ampersand) operator, e.g., scanf("%d", &num);
\n is a newline escape sequence used inside printf to move the cursor to the next line.
Always include #include <stdio.h> at the top of your program when using printf or scanf.

detailed.explanation:
In C, the two most basic tools for interacting with users are `printf` and `scanf`. Both are functions provided by the standard input/output library, which you include at the top of your program using `#include <stdio.h>`. Without this line, the compiler will not recognise these functions.

`printf` stands for *print formatted*. It is used to display text and variable values on the screen. You provide a format string in double quotes, which can contain plain text and format specifiers. For example, `printf("Age: %d\n", age);` will print the value of the integer variable `age` in place of `%d`. The `\n` at the end moves the cursor to the next line.

`scanf` stands for *scan formatted*. It reads input typed by the user and stores it in a variable. The key rule is that you must pass the *address* of the variable using the `&` operator. For example, `scanf("%d", &age);` reads an integer and stores it at the memory location of `age`. Forgetting `&` is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Format specifiers are codes that begin with `%` and indicate the data type. The most common ones are: `%d` for `int`, `%f` for `float`, `%lf` for `double`, `%c` for `char`, and `%s` for strings. Using the wrong specifier can cause unexpected output or even a crash.

Escape sequences like `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab), and `\\` (backslash) are special character combinations used inside string literals to control formatting. They are written with a backslash prefix and are interpreted by the compiler, not printed literally.

definitions.meaning: A standard library function in C used to print formatted text and variable values to the console.
A standard library function in C used to read formatted input from the keyboard and store it in variables.
A placeholder starting with % used inside printf and scanf to indicate the data type, e.g., %d for integer.
A combination of a backslash and a character used inside strings to represent special characters, like \n for newline.
An operator used in scanf to pass the memory address of a variable so the function knows where to store the input.
The standard input/output header file in C that must be included to use printf and scanf.

points: Always write #include <stdio.h> at the top of any C program that uses printf or scanf.
Use %d for int, %f for float, %lf for double, %c for char, and %s for strings.
In scanf, always use the & operator before a variable name (except for strings/arrays).
\n inside a printf string moves output to the next line; it does not print a visible character.
printf returns the number of characters printed; scanf returns the number of items successfully read — these are rarely used by beginners but good to know for exams.
Mismatched format specifiers and variable types lead to undefined behaviour — always match them correctly.
Multiple values can be read in one scanf call: scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); reads two integers.
For printing a float with 2 decimal places, use %.2f inside printf, e.g., printf("%.2f", price);.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the & operator in scanf, e.g., writing scanf("%d", num) instead of scanf("%d", &num). This causes undefined behaviour because scanf does not know where to store the value.
Using the wrong format specifier, such as using %d to read or print a float variable. Always match %f with float and %d with int.
Forgetting #include <stdio.h> at the top of the program, which causes a compilation error because the compiler cannot find the definitions of printf and scanf.

topics.title: Decision Making with if-else and switch

lesson.summary: Decision making in C uses if-else statements and switch statements to execute different blocks of code based on conditions.
shortNotes: The if statement executes a block only when its condition is true.
The if-else statement provides an alternative block when the condition is false.
else-if ladder allows checking multiple conditions in sequence.
The switch statement matches an expression against constant integer or character cases.
Every case in switch should end with break to prevent fall-through to the next case.
The default case in switch acts like the final else and runs when no case matches.

detailed.explanation:
In C programming, decision making means choosing which block of code to run based on a condition. The simplest form is the `if` statement: if the condition inside parentheses evaluates to true (non-zero), the body executes; otherwise it is skipped entirely. This lets your program react differently to different inputs.

The `if-else` statement extends this by providing a second block that runs when the condition is false. You can chain multiple conditions using `else if`, forming a ladder. The program checks each condition from top to bottom and executes only the first block whose condition is true; if none match, the optional final `else` block runs.

The `switch` statement is used when you want to compare one variable or expression against several fixed constant values. C evaluates the expression once and jumps to the matching `case` label. Without a `break` at the end of a case, execution continues into the next case — this is called fall-through, and it is a very common source of bugs for beginners.

Choosing between `if-else` and `switch` depends on the situation. Use `switch` when comparing a single integer or character variable against known constant values; it is cleaner and sometimes faster. Use `if-else` when your conditions involve ranges, logical operators, or floating-point comparisons, because `switch` cannot handle those.

definitions.meaning: An expression that evaluates to either true (non-zero) or false (zero) in C.
A control structure that executes a block of code only when a specified condition is true.
The optional part of an if-else statement that executes when the condition is false.
A chain of if-else if-else blocks used to test multiple mutually exclusive conditions in order.
A control structure that matches an integer or character expression against a list of constant case labels and jumps to the matching one.
A constant value inside a switch block that the expression is compared against.
A keyword that exits the switch block immediately, preventing fall-through to the next case.
An optional label in switch that runs when no other case matches, similar to a final else.
The behavior in switch where execution continues into the next case if break is missing.

points: In C, zero is treated as false and any non-zero value is treated as true in a condition.
Curly braces are optional when an if or else body has only one statement, but always using them prevents bugs.
The switch expression must evaluate to an integer type (int, char, short, etc.); float and string are not allowed.
Each case value must be a compile-time integer constant; you cannot use a variable as a case label.
If you forget break in a switch case, all subsequent cases run until a break or the end of the switch — exam favorite question.
The default case can be placed anywhere inside switch, but placing it last is the standard convention.
Nested if-else statements are allowed but deep nesting makes code hard to read; prefer else-if ladder or switch when possible.
Using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison) inside an if condition is a very common and hard-to-spot bug.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: Include standard input/output header.
Line 3: Start of main function.
Line 4-5: Declare integer variable marks and character variable grade.
Line 7-8: Prompt user and read marks using scanf.
Line 10-20: if-else ladder checks marks from highest to lowest range and assigns a character grade. Only the first matching condition executes.
Line 22: Print the grade determined by the if-else ladder.
Line 24-38: switch statement matches the value of grade against character constants. Each case prints a message and ends with break to stop fall-through. The default case handles any unmatched value (here it would print Fail for grade F).
Line 40: Return 0 to indicate successful program execution.

commonMistakes: Writing = instead of == in a condition (e.g., if (x = 5) always evaluates to true and assigns 5 to x instead of comparing).
Forgetting break at the end of a switch case, causing fall-through where multiple case blocks execute unintentionally.
Using a float or a string expression in a switch statement, which is not allowed in C and causes a compilation error.

scenes.title: Introduction to Decision Making in C

steps.say: Hello everyone! Today we are going to learn about decision making in C, which is how your program chooses what to do based on different situations.
Think of it like a crossroads. The program looks at a condition and picks the right path to follow.
If the condition is false, it takes a different path. C gives us two main tools for this: the if-else statement and the switch statement.
Let us look at the if-else statement. We write the keyword if, then the condition inside round brackets.
Inside the curly braces we write the code that runs when the condition is true.
Then we write else and another block that runs when the condition is false.
For example, if marks are greater than or equal to 40, we print Pass, otherwise we print Fail. The program checks the condition once and picks exactly one block to run.
When you have more than two choices, you can chain conditions using else-if. This is called an else-if ladder.
The program checks conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block that is true.
If that is not true, it checks the next condition.
And finally, if none of the conditions match, the else block runs. Remember, only one block ever runs in a ladder.
Now let us look at the switch statement. It is great when you are comparing one variable against several fixed values.
We write switch, then the variable inside brackets. Inside the block we write case labels.
Each case has a constant value. The program jumps to the matching case. Always end each case with break, otherwise execution falls into the next case.
The default case runs when no case matches. It works just like a final else.
Let us quickly recap what we learned today. The if statement runs a block only when the condition is true.
The else-if ladder checks multiple conditions in order and runs only the first matching block.
The switch statement matches one expression against constant values. Always use break to stop fall-through.

write.content: switch: use break to stop fall-through

steps.say: Use switch for fixed constant values, and use if-else for ranges or complex conditions. Great work today, see you in the next lesson!

lesson.summary: Loops in C (for, while, do-while) allow a block of code to execute repeatedly based on a condition, reducing redundancy and making programs efficient.
shortNotes: A loop repeats a block of code as long as a given condition is true.
The `for` loop is best when the number of iterations is known in advance.
The `while` loop checks the condition before executing the body (entry-controlled).
The `do-while` loop executes the body at least once before checking the condition (exit-controlled).
`break` exits a loop immediately; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration.
An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition never becomes false — always update the loop variable.

detailed.explanation:
A **loop** is a control flow structure that repeats a set of statements multiple times. Instead of writing the same code ten times, you write it once inside a loop and tell the program how many times (or under what condition) to repeat it. C provides three types of loops: `for`, `while`, and `do-while`.

The **`for` loop** is the most compact. Its header contains three parts separated by semicolons: initialization, condition, and update. For example, `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)` starts `i` at 0, runs while `i` is less than 5, and increments `i` after each iteration. It is ideal when you know the exact number of repetitions beforehand.

The **`while` loop** first checks the condition, and only if it is true does it execute the body. Because the check happens at the top, if the condition is false from the very beginning the body never runs. It is useful when the number of iterations is not known in advance — for example, reading input until the user types -1.

The **`do-while` loop** is similar to `while`, but the condition is checked *after* the body executes. This guarantees the body runs at least once. The syntax ends with a semicolon after the closing parenthesis: `do { ... } while (condition);`. A classic use case is a menu-driven program where you always want to show the menu at least once.

All three loops support `break` (exit the loop immediately) and `continue` (skip the remaining statements in the current iteration and go to the next). Nested loops are also allowed — a loop inside another loop — which is commonly used for patterns and matrix operations.

definitions.meaning: A programming construct that repeats a block of statements until a specified condition becomes false.
An entry-controlled loop with initialization, condition, and update all in one line; best when the iteration count is known.
An entry-controlled loop that checks its condition before each iteration; the body may never execute if the condition starts false.
An exit-controlled loop that executes its body first, then checks the condition; the body always runs at least once.
A variable used to control how many times a loop executes, typically initialized before and updated inside or in the loop header.
A loop whose condition never becomes false, causing the program to run forever; usually a bug caused by forgetting to update the loop variable.
A statement that immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch.
A statement that skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps to the next iteration's condition check.

points: The `for` loop syntax is: `for (init; condition; update) { body }` — all three parts are optional but the two semicolons are mandatory.
The `while` loop is entry-controlled: if the condition is false at the start, the body executes zero times.
The `do-while` loop is exit-controlled: the body always executes at least once regardless of the condition.
Always ensure the loop variable is updated; missing the update step is the most common cause of infinite loops.
In a `for` loop you can declare the counter variable inside the header (`int i = 0`); its scope is limited to the loop in C99 and later.
`break` inside a nested loop exits only the innermost loop, not all loops.
For exam questions: if asked 'which loop guarantees at least one execution', the answer is `do-while`.
The `continue` statement in a `for` loop still executes the update expression before re-checking the condition.

Line 13-18: while loop — i is set to 1 before the loop; condition i <= 5 is checked first; body prints i and increments it; same output.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the loop variable inside a `while` or `do-while` loop, causing an infinite loop (e.g., writing `while (i < 5)` but never writing `i++` inside the body).
Using a semicolon immediately after the `for` or `while` header, like `for (i=0; i<5; i++);` — this creates an empty loop body and the intended block never executes as part of the loop.
Off-by-one errors: using `<` vs `<=` incorrectly — for example, `for (i=1; i<5; i++)` prints only 1 to 4, not 1 to 5; always trace through the first and last values manually.

Restarts the loop from the initialization

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an entry-controlled loop?

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a `while` loop and a `do-while` loop in C.
questions.answer: A while loop is entry-controlled: it checks the condition before executing the body, so if the condition is false initially, the body never runs. A do-while loop is exit-controlled: it executes the body first and checks the condition afterward, guaranteeing the body runs at least once.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is where the condition is evaluated — before or after the body — which determines the minimum number of times the body can execute (zero for while, one for do-while).

questions.prompt: What is an infinite loop? Give one common reason it occurs in C.

questions.explanation: Without updating the loop variable, the condition remains true forever. Always check that the loop variable changes in a way that will eventually make the condition false.

lesson.summary: A function in C is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be called multiple times to avoid code repetition.
shortNotes: A function has a return type, a name, optional parameters, and a body enclosed in curly braces.
The `main()` function is the entry point of every C program and is called automatically by the system.
Functions must be declared before use via a function prototype, or defined before the calling function.
Use `return` to send a value back to the caller; use `void` if nothing is returned.
Arguments are passed by value by default, meaning the function gets a copy of the variable.
Breaking a program into functions makes code readable, reusable, and easier to debug.

detailed.explanation:
A **function** in C is a self-contained block of statements that carries out a well-defined job. Instead of writing the same logic repeatedly, you write it once inside a function and call it whenever needed. This is the core idea behind structured programming.

Every C function has four parts: a **return type** (what kind of value it gives back), a **name** (how you call it), a **parameter list** (input values it needs, or empty parentheses if none), and a **body** (the statements inside `{ }`). For example, `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }` defines a function named `add` that takes two integers and returns their sum.

Before you call a function that is defined later in the file, you must provide a **function prototype** — a one-line declaration ending with a semicolon, such as `int add(int a, int b);`. This tells the compiler what to expect. If the function is defined above `main()`, the prototype is not strictly required but is considered good practice.

When a function is called, control jumps to the function body, executes the statements, and then returns to the line after the call. If the return type is not `void`, the `return` statement sends a value back. C passes arguments **by value**, so changes inside the function do not affect the original variable in the caller.

Choosing good function names and keeping each function focused on a single task is a key habit in professional C programming. Functions also make testing easier because you can check each piece of logic independently.

definitions.meaning: A named, reusable block of C code that performs a specific task and may return a value.
The data type of the value the function sends back to the caller (e.g., int, float, void).
A variable listed in the function definition that receives input when the function is called.
The actual value passed to a function when it is called.
A forward declaration of a function (return type, name, parameter types) placed before it is used, ending with a semicolon.
A keyword used as return type when a function does not return any value.
Exits the current function and optionally sends a value back to the caller.
The default argument-passing method in C where a copy of the variable is passed, not the original.

points: Syntax: `return_type function_name(parameter_list) { body }` — memorise this structure.
A function prototype must match the definition exactly in return type and parameter types.
If a function returns `int` but you forget the `return` statement, the behaviour is undefined.
A `void` function can use `return;` (with no value) to exit early.
Local variables declared inside a function exist only while that function is executing (automatic storage duration).
Recursion is allowed in C — a function can call itself — but every recursive call needs a base case to stop.
The `main()` function returns `int`; returning `0` signals successful execution to the operating system.
Exam tip: distinguish between formal parameters (in the definition) and actual arguments (in the call).

Using the wrong return type (e.g., declaring `void` but trying to `return` a value, or declaring `int` but forgetting to `return` anything).
Expecting a function to modify the caller's variable through normal parameters — since C uses call by value, the original variable is not changed; pointers are needed for that.

The function receives a copy of the argument's value.
The caller receives the function's local variables.
The function modifies the original variable directly.
questions.explanation: Call by value means a copy of the actual argument is passed. Changes inside the function do not affect the original variable in the caller.

The first prototype in the file

An argument is the actual value supplied when the function is called, for example `5` in `square(5)`. The argument is copied into the parameter when the function executes.
questions.explanation: Parameters belong to the function signature; arguments are provided by the caller. This distinction is commonly tested in exams.

questions.prompt: Why is it good practice to use function prototypes in a C program?
questions.answer: A function prototype tells the compiler the return type and parameter types of a function before it is defined. This allows the compiler to check that calls to the function use the correct number and types of arguments, catching type mismatches at compile time instead of causing bugs at runtime.
questions.explanation: Prototypes enable compile-time type checking. Without them, the compiler cannot verify that function calls are correct, leading to hard-to-find bugs.

lesson.summary: An array in C is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations, accessed using an index.
shortNotes: An array stores multiple values of the same type under one variable name.
Array indexing in C starts at 0, so the last element is at index n-1.
Declaration syntax: data_type array_name[size]; e.g., int marks[5];
Arrays are stored in contiguous memory; the name itself holds the base address.
Array size must be a positive integer constant at the time of declaration (in basic C).
Out-of-bounds access is undefined behaviour and a very common bug in C.

detailed.explanation:
An **array** is a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements that all share the same data type. Instead of declaring five separate variables like `marks1`, `marks2`, … `marks5`, you declare one array: `int marks[5];`. All five integers are stored back-to-back in memory, which makes accessing them fast and predictable.

The elements of an array are accessed using an **index** (also called a subscript) inside square brackets. C uses **zero-based indexing**, meaning the first element is `marks[0]`, the second is `marks[1]`, and so on up to `marks[4]` for a size-5 array. Trying to read or write `marks[5]` goes beyond the allocated memory and causes undefined behaviour.

Arrays can be **initialized** at the time of declaration. For example, `int marks[5] = {90, 85, 78, 92, 88};` fills all five slots immediately. If you provide fewer values than the size, the remaining elements are automatically set to zero. You can also omit the size and let the compiler count: `int marks[] = {90, 85, 78};` creates an array of size 3.

To process every element of an array you typically use a `for` loop. The loop counter serves as the index, running from `0` to `n-1`. This pattern — declare, initialize, loop — is the backbone of almost every array operation you will write in C.

definitions.meaning: A fixed-size sequence of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations.
An integer value inside square brackets used to identify a specific element in an array; starts at 0 in C.
The memory address of the first element of the array; the array name itself represents this address.
Assigning values to array elements at the time of declaration using a comma-separated list inside curly braces.
Memory locations that are adjacent to each other without any gaps, which is how array elements are stored.
What happens in C when you access an array element outside its valid index range; the result is unpredictable and dangerous.

formulas.name: Address of element i
formulas.note: Shows why array access is O(1) — the CPU computes the exact address directly from the index.

formulas.name: Valid index range
formulas.note: For an array declared with size n, valid indices run from 0 to n minus 1.

formulas.name: Total memory used
formulas.note: For example, int arr[10] uses 10 * 4 = 40 bytes on most systems.

points: Always remember: for an array of size n, valid indices are 0 to n-1. Writing to index n is a common and dangerous mistake.
In C, the compiler does NOT check array bounds at runtime — it is your responsibility to stay within limits.
When you pass an array to a function, you are actually passing its base address (a pointer), so changes inside the function affect the original array.
A partially initialized array like int a[5] = {1, 2}; sets a[0]=1, a[1]=2, and a[2], a[3], a[4] to 0 automatically.
sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]) is a common idiom to find the number of elements in an array inside the same function where it is declared.
Multi-dimensional arrays (e.g., int matrix[3][4];) are simply arrays of arrays and are stored row-by-row in memory.
Exam tip: If asked for the memory address of element i, use: base + i * sizeof(type). This is a frequently tested formula.
Global and static arrays are zero-initialized by default; local (automatic) arrays contain garbage values if not explicitly initialized.

Line 6: Loop counter variable i.

Forgetting that local arrays are uninitialized: writing int arr[5]; and reading values from it without assigning them first gives garbage output.
Using = instead of a loop to copy arrays: writing arr2 = arr1 does NOT copy array contents in C; you must copy element by element (or use memcpy).

options: The compiler shows an error and stops
The element wraps around to the beginning

questions.prompt: What will be the value of a[2] after this declaration? int a[5] = {1, 2};

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of the base address of an array in C.
questions.answer: The base address is the memory address of the first element (index 0) of the array. In C, the array name itself holds this base address. The address of any element i is calculated as base_address + i * sizeof(data_type), which is why array access takes constant time regardless of the index.
questions.explanation: Understanding the base address helps explain how C computes the location of any element in O(1) time and why the array name behaves like a pointer.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between array declaration and array initialization in C? Give a short example of each.
questions.answer: Declaration allocates memory for the array without assigning values, e.g., int marks[5]; — this reserves space for 5 integers but their values are undefined (garbage) for local arrays. Initialization assigns specific values at the time of declaration, e.g., int marks[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; — this both allocates memory and fills it with known values.
questions.explanation: Students often confuse declaring an array with initializing it. Uninitialized local arrays contain garbage values which is a very common source of bugs.

The second loop compares every remaining element with largest; if a bigger element is found, largest is updated. After the loop, the true maximum is printed.
