The `else` block covers the only remaining case: the number is exactly 0. Only one of these three blocks will execute for any given input.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are going to learn about conditional statements in Python. These let your program make decisions, just like you do in real life.
Think about this: if it rains, you carry an umbrella. Otherwise, you do not. A program works the same way.

write.content: If condition is True → run this block

steps.say: Python gives us three keywords for this: if, elif, and else. Let us see how each one works.
Here is the simplest form. We write if, then our condition, then a colon. The indented line below runs only when the condition is true.
So we check if marks are greater than or equal to 40.
If that is true, we print Pass. Notice the four spaces of indentation — that is how Python knows this line belongs to the if block.
Now we add else. If the condition was false, Python comes here instead and prints Fail.
What if we need to check more than two possibilities? That is where elif comes in. It stands for else if.
Python checks conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true.
If marks are 75 or above, we print grade A.
If not, we check the next condition with elif. If marks are 40 or above, we print grade B.
And if none of those matched, else catches it and prints Fail. Only one block ever runs.
Let me quickly show you the three mistakes beginners make most often. First, using a single equals sign instead of double equals inside a condition.
Second, forgetting the colon at the end of the if or else line. That gives you a syntax error immediately.
Third, wrong indentation. Python does not use curly braces, so your indentation must be consistent — use four spaces every time.
Great work! Let us quickly recap what we covered today.
Use if to run code when a condition is true. Use elif to check more conditions. Use else to handle everything else.
Always use double equals for comparison, end each condition line with a colon, and indent your blocks with four spaces.
Python runs only the first matching block and skips the rest. Now try writing your own conditional program and experiment with different inputs. Good luck!

write.content: Only ONE block runs per chain

lesson.summary: Loops in Python allow you to repeatedly execute a block of code using `for` and `while` statements, making it easy to automate repetitive tasks.
shortNotes: A `for` loop iterates over a sequence such as a list, string, or range of numbers.
A `while` loop keeps running as long as a given condition remains True.
The `range(start, stop, step)` function generates a sequence of numbers for use in loops.
Use `break` to exit a loop immediately and `continue` to skip the current iteration.
Loops can be nested — one loop placed inside another — to handle multi-dimensional problems.
An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition never becomes False; always ensure a proper exit condition.

detailed.explanation:
A loop is a control flow structure that lets you run a block of code multiple times without rewriting it. Python provides two main types of loops: the `for` loop and the `while` loop. They save time and reduce errors when you need to process collections of data or repeat actions a certain number of times.

The `for` loop is used to iterate over any sequence — a list, a tuple, a string, or a range of numbers. The syntax is `for variable in sequence:` followed by an indented block. For example, `for i in range(5):` will run the block five times with `i` taking values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. The `range()` function is very commonly used here; `range(start, stop, step)` gives you fine control over the sequence of numbers.

The `while` loop runs its block as long as a condition is `True`. The syntax is `while condition:` followed by an indented block. You must make sure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition `False`, otherwise the program will run forever — this is called an infinite loop.

Python also provides two special keywords to control loop execution. `break` immediately exits the loop, while `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps back to the top of the loop. Both work inside `for` and `while` loops.

Loops can be placed inside other loops — this is called nesting. A nested loop is useful for working with tables, matrices, or any problem that has two levels of repetition. Be careful with nested loops as they can slow your program down if the sequences are very large.

definitions.meaning: A loop that iterates over each item in a sequence (list, string, range, etc.) one by one.
A loop that repeats its block of code as long as a specified condition evaluates to True.
A built-in Python function that generates a sequence of integers, commonly used with for loops.
A keyword that immediately terminates the loop and transfers control to the statement after the loop.
A keyword that skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and moves to the next iteration.
A loop whose condition never becomes False, causing the program to run endlessly.
A loop that is placed inside another loop, allowing iteration over multi-dimensional structures.
The variable in a for loop that takes the value of each element in the sequence during each iteration.

formulas.name: range with start, stop, step
formulas.note: Generates numbers from start up to (but not including) stop, incrementing by step each time. Default start is 0 and default step is 1.

points: The `for` loop is best when you know in advance how many times you want to iterate.
The `while` loop is best when the number of iterations depends on a condition that changes during execution.
In `range(stop)`, the stop value is EXCLUDED — `range(5)` gives 0,1,2,3,4, not 5.
`break` exits the entire loop; `continue` only skips the current iteration.
Always update the loop variable or condition inside a `while` loop to avoid infinite loops.
Python uses indentation (4 spaces or 1 tab) to define the loop body — incorrect indentation causes errors.
A `for` loop can also have an `else` clause that runs after the loop finishes normally (without a `break`).
Nested loops multiply the number of iterations — two loops of 10 each means 100 total iterations.

codeExample.code:
# ---- Loops in Python: Complete Example ----

# 1. Basic for loop using range
print("Counting from 1 to 5:")
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

# 2. for loop iterating over a list
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]
print("\nFruits in the list:")
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# 3. while loop
print("\nCountdown:")
count = 5
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Go!")

# 4. Using break
print("\nSearch for mango:")
for fruit in fruits:
    if fruit == "mango":
        print("Found mango! Stopping.")
        break
    print("Not mango:", fruit)

# 5. Using continue
print("\nSkip banana:")
for fruit in fruits:
    if fruit == "banana":
        continue
    print(fruit)

# 6. Nested loop — multiplication table (2 and 3)
print("\nMini multiplication table:")
for row in range(2, 4):
    for col in range(1, 6):
        print(row, "x", col, "=", row * col)
codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: Comment describing the program.
Line 3-5: A for loop using range(1,6) counts from 1 to 5 (6 is excluded). Each value of i is printed.
Line 7-10: A for loop iterates directly over the list 'fruits'. The variable 'fruit' holds each element in turn.

lesson.summary: A function in Python is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task, helping you avoid repetition and organise your programs clearly.
shortNotes: A function is defined using the `def` keyword followed by the function name and parentheses.
Functions can accept input values called parameters and return output using the `return` statement.
A function must be defined before it is called in the program.
If no `return` statement is used, the function returns `None` by default.
Default parameter values let you call a function without always passing every argument.
Functions improve code reusability, readability, and make debugging easier.

detailed.explanation:
A **function** is a block of code that runs only when it is called. Instead of writing the same logic again and again, you wrap it inside a function and call it whenever needed. This is one of the most important ideas in programming.

You define a function using the `def` keyword, followed by a name, parentheses `()`, and a colon `:`. The body of the function is indented. For example: `def greet():` starts a function named `greet`. You run it by writing `greet()` anywhere after the definition.

Functions can receive data through **parameters** listed inside the parentheses. When you call the function, you pass actual values called **arguments**. For example, `def greet(name):` defines a parameter `name`, and `greet('Riya')` passes the argument `'Riya'`.

The `return` statement sends a value back to the place where the function was called. Once `return` is executed, the function stops immediately. If there is no `return`, Python automatically returns `None`.

You can also define **default parameter values** like `def greet(name='Student'):`. If the caller does not pass an argument, the default value is used. This makes functions more flexible and convenient to use.

definitions.meaning: A named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task when called.
The Python keyword used to define (create) a function.
A variable listed in the function definition that receives a value when the function is called.
The actual value passed to a function when it is called.
A statement inside a function that sends a value back to the caller and ends the function.
A parameter that has a preset value used when no argument is supplied by the caller.
The line of code that executes a function by writing its name followed by parentheses.

points: Always use the `def` keyword to define a function; forgetting it causes a SyntaxError.
The function body must be indented consistently (4 spaces is the Python standard).
A function with no `return` statement returns `None`; do not assume it returns 0 or an empty string.
Parameters and arguments must match in number unless default values are provided.
You can have multiple `return` statements in a function (e.g., inside if-else), but only one executes per call.
A function can call another function — this is called function composition.
In exams, trace the flow carefully: identify where the function is defined vs where it is called.
Default arguments must come after non-default arguments in the parameter list, or Python raises a SyntaxError.

codeExample.code:
# Function with no parameters
def greet():
    print('Hello! Welcome to Python.')

# Function with a parameter
def greet_user(name):
    print('Hello,', name + '!')

# Function with a default parameter
def greet_default(name='Student'):
    print('Hello,', name + '!')

# Function that returns a value
def add(a, b):
    result = a + b
    return result

# Calling the functions
greet()
greet_user('Riya')
greet_default()
greet_default('Amit')

total = add(10, 5)
print('Sum:', total)
codeExample.explanation:
Line 2-3: `greet` is a simple function with no parameters; it just prints a welcome message.
Line 6-7: `greet_user` accepts one parameter `name` and uses it in the print statement.
Line 10-11: `greet_default` has a default value `'Student'` for `name`; if no argument is given, it uses that default.
Line 14-16: `add` takes two parameters `a` and `b`, computes their sum, stores it in `result`, and returns it.
Line 19: Calling `greet()` runs the first function and prints the welcome message.
Line 20: Calling `greet_user('Riya')` passes 'Riya' as the argument, so it prints 'Hello, Riya!'.
Line 21: Calling `greet_default()` uses the default value, printing 'Hello, Student!'.
Line 22: Calling `greet_default('Amit')` overrides the default, printing 'Hello, Amit!'.
Line 24-25: `add(10, 5)` returns 15, which is stored in `total` and then printed as 'Sum: 15'.

commonMistakes: Calling a function before defining it: Python reads code top to bottom, so defining the function after the call causes a NameError.
Forgetting to use `return` and expecting the function to give back a value: without `return`, the function returns `None`, causing unexpected results when you try to use the output.
Mixing up parameters and arguments: changing a parameter name inside the function does not affect the variable outside unless the value is returned and stored.

lesson.summary: Lists and tuples are Python's most common sequence types — lists are mutable (changeable) while tuples are immutable (fixed), and both let you store ordered collections of items.
shortNotes: A list is created with square brackets [ ] and can be changed after creation.
A tuple is created with parentheses ( ) and cannot be changed after creation.
Both lists and tuples are ordered, indexed from 0, and allow duplicate values.
Common list methods: append(), remove(), pop(), sort(), len().
Tuples are faster than lists and are used when data should not change.
Negative indexing works on both: -1 gives the last element.

detailed.explanation:
A **list** in Python is a collection of items stored in a single variable. You create a list using square brackets, like `fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'mango']`. Lists are **mutable**, meaning you can add, remove, or change items after the list is created. This makes them very flexible for everyday programming tasks.

A **tuple** is similar to a list but uses parentheses: `colors = ('red', 'green', 'blue')`. The key difference is that tuples are **immutable** — once you create a tuple, you cannot change its contents. This is useful when you want to protect data from accidental changes, such as storing the days of the week or GPS coordinates.

Both lists and tuples support **indexing** and **slicing**. Indexing starts at 0, so `fruits[0]` gives `'apple'`. You can also use negative indices: `fruits[-1]` gives the last item. Slicing lets you get a sub-section: `fruits[0:2]` gives `['apple', 'banana']`.

Lists come with many built-in methods. `append()` adds an item at the end, `remove()` deletes a specific value, `pop()` removes by index, and `sort()` arranges items in order. Tuples have only two methods: `count()` and `index()`, because they cannot be modified.

Choosing between a list and a tuple depends on your use case. If your data needs to change, use a list. If it should remain constant throughout the program, a tuple is the safer and slightly faster choice.

definitions.meaning: An ordered, mutable collection of items created using square brackets, e.g., [1, 2, 3].
An ordered, immutable collection of items created using parentheses, e.g., (1, 2, 3).
An object whose contents can be changed after it is created.
An object whose contents cannot be changed after it is created.
Accessing an individual element in a sequence using its position number, starting from 0.
Extracting a portion of a sequence using a start and end index, e.g., my_list[1:3].
A list method that adds a single element to the end of the list.
Accessing elements from the end of a sequence; -1 refers to the last element.

points: Lists use [ ] and tuples use ( ) — this distinction is commonly tested in exams.
Index always starts at 0; the last valid index is len(sequence) - 1.
Trying to modify a tuple raises a TypeError — remember this for debugging questions.
len() works on both lists and tuples to get the number of elements.
A single-element tuple must have a trailing comma: (5,) — without the comma Python treats it as just (5), which is an integer.
List slicing syntax: list[start:stop:step] — stop index is excluded.
Tuples can be used as dictionary keys because they are immutable; lists cannot.
append() adds one item; extend() adds multiple items from another iterable to a list.

codeExample.code:
# Lists and Tuples in Python

# --- LISTS ---
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'mango']
print('Original list:', fruits)

# Accessing elements
print('First fruit:', fruits[0])
print('Last fruit:', fruits[-1])

# Adding and removing elements
fruits.append('grapes')
print('After append:', fruits)

fruits.remove('banana')
print('After remove:', fruits)

# Slicing
print('Slice [0:2]:', fruits[0:2])

# Sorting
numbers = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]
numbers.sort()
print('Sorted numbers:', numbers)

# --- TUPLES ---
days = ('Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday')
print('\nTuple:', days)
print('Second day:', days[1])
print('Number of days:', len(days))

# Tuple count and index methods
scores = (10, 20, 10, 30, 10)
print('Count of 10:', scores.count(10))
print('Index of 20:', scores.index(20))

# Trying to modify a tuple (this will raise an error)
try:
    days[0] = 'Sunday'
except TypeError as e:
    print('\nError:', e)

# Single-element tuple
single = (42,)
print('\nSingle-element tuple:', single)
print('Type:', type(single))
codeExample.explanation:
Line 3: We create a list called 'fruits' with three string items using square brackets.
Line 4: We print the full list.
Line 7: fruits[0] accesses the first element ('apple') using index 0.
Line 8: fruits[-1] uses negative indexing to access the last element ('mango').
Line 11: append('grapes') adds 'grapes' to the end of the list.
Line 14: remove('banana') finds and deletes 'banana' from the list.
Line 17: fruits[0:2] returns a new list from index 0 up to (but not including) index 2.
Line 20-22: We create a numbers list and call sort() to arrange it in ascending order.
Line 25: We create a tuple called 'days' using parentheses.
Line 26-27: Indexing and len() work the same as with lists.
Line 31-33: count(10) returns how many times 10 appears; index(20) returns the position of 20.
Line 36-39: We try to change a tuple element inside a try-except block — Python raises a TypeError, which we catch and print.
Line 42-44: A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma; we verify its type is 'tuple'.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the trailing comma in a single-element tuple: writing (5) gives an integer, not a tuple — you must write (5,).
Trying to change a tuple element directly (e.g., my_tuple[0] = 10) and being confused by the TypeError — remember, tuples are immutable.
Confusing the stop index in slicing: my_list[1:3] returns elements at index 1 and 2 only — index 3 is NOT included.

lesson.summary: Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs and sets store unique unordered elements, making both powerful tools for organising and processing data in Python.
shortNotes: A dictionary is a collection of key-value pairs written with curly braces, e.g. {'name': 'Riya', 'age': 20}.
Keys in a dictionary must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples); values can be anything.
A set is an unordered collection of unique elements; duplicates are automatically removed.
Use dict[key] or dict.get(key) to access values; use set.add() to insert into a set.
Common dictionary methods: keys(), values(), items(), get(), pop(), update().
Common set operations: union (|), intersection (&), difference (-), and issubset().

detailed.explanation:
A **dictionary** in Python is a collection that stores data in **key-value pairs**. You create one using curly braces with a colon separating each key from its value, like `student = {'name': 'Riya', 'marks': 95}`. Dictionaries are very useful when you want to look up information quickly using a meaningful label (the key) instead of a numeric index.

You can access a value using `student['name']` or the safer `student.get('name')` which returns `None` instead of raising an error if the key does not exist. You can add or update entries simply by assigning: `student['grade'] = 'A'`. To remove a key, use `student.pop('marks')`. The methods `keys()`, `values()`, and `items()` let you loop over the dictionary easily.

A **set** is an unordered collection that **never stores duplicates**. You create a set with curly braces too, but without key-value pairs: `fruits = {'apple', 'mango', 'apple'}` automatically becomes `{'apple', 'mango'}`. To create an **empty set** you must write `set()` — writing `{}` creates an empty dictionary, not a set.

Sets support powerful mathematical operations. `A | B` gives the union (all elements from both), `A & B` gives the intersection (only common elements), and `A - B` gives the difference (elements in A but not in B). These are very handy for tasks like finding common students in two class lists.

Choose a **dictionary** when your data has labels or attributes (like a student record). Choose a **set** when you only care about unique membership, such as removing duplicates from a list or checking whether an item exists quickly.

definitions.meaning: A mutable, ordered (Python 3.7+) collection of key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces, where each key is unique.
The unique, immutable identifier used to access a value in a dictionary, such as a string or number.
The data associated with a key in a dictionary; can be any Python object.
An unordered, mutable collection of unique elements enclosed in curly braces, with no duplicates allowed.
A set operation (|) that returns all unique elements from two sets combined.
A set operation (&) that returns only the elements that appear in both sets.
A set operation (-) that returns elements present in the first set but not in the second.

points: Dictionaries maintain insertion order in Python 3.7 and later — this is important to remember for exams.
Dictionary keys must be immutable: strings, integers, and tuples are valid keys; lists are NOT.
Accessing a key that does not exist with dict[key] raises a KeyError; use dict.get(key) to avoid this.
An empty set must be created with set(), not {} — {} always creates an empty dictionary.
Sets are unordered, so you cannot access set elements by index or slice.
The in keyword works for both dictionaries (checks keys) and sets (checks membership) and is very fast.
Use dict.items() in a for loop to get both key and value at the same time: for k, v in d.items().
Duplicates added to a set are silently ignored — this is useful for de-duplicating a list.

codeExample.code:
# --- DICTIONARIES ---
# Create a student dictionary
student = {
    'name': 'Arjun',
    'branch': 'CSE',
    'marks': 88
}

# Access values
print(student['name'])          # Arjun
print(student.get('grade', 'N/A'))  # N/A (key missing, default returned)

# Add / update an entry
student['grade'] = 'A'
print(student)

# Loop through key-value pairs
for key, value in student.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

# Remove a key
student.pop('marks')
print(student)

# --- SETS ---
# Create a set (duplicates removed automatically)
attendance = {'Priya', 'Arjun', 'Meera', 'Priya'}
print(attendance)   # 'Priya' appears only once

# Add and remove elements
attendance.add('Rohit')
attendance.discard('Meera')   # no error if element missing
print(attendance)

# Set operations
set_a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
set_b = {3, 4, 5, 6}

print(set_a | set_b)   # Union:        {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
print(set_a & set_b)   # Intersection: {3, 4}
print(set_a - set_b)   # Difference:   {1, 2}

# Check membership
if 'Arjun' in attendance:
    print("Arjun is present")

# De-duplicate a list using a set
scores = [90, 85, 90, 78, 85, 100]
unique_scores = list(set(scores))
print(unique_scores)
codeExample.explanation:
Line 3-7: We create a dictionary called student with three key-value pairs — name, branch, and marks.
Line 10: student['name'] retrieves the value for the key 'name', printing 'Arjun'.
Line 11: student.get('grade', 'N/A') safely looks up 'grade'; since it does not exist, it returns the default 'N/A' instead of raising an error.
Line 14: Assigning to a new key 'grade' adds it to the dictionary.
Line 17-18: dict.items() returns each key-value pair as a tuple; we unpack it into key and value inside the for loop.
Line 21: pop('marks') removes the 'marks' key and its value from the dictionary.
Line 25: We create a set with a duplicate 'Priya'; Python keeps only one copy automatically.
Line 29: add() inserts 'Rohit' into the set.
Line 30: discard() removes 'Meera' safely — unlike remove(), it does not raise an error if the element is absent.
Line 34-36: We demonstrate union (|), intersection (&), and difference (-) operations on two sets.
Line 39-40: The in keyword checks if 'Arjun' is a member of the attendance set.
Line 43-44: Converting a list to a set removes all duplicates; converting back with list() gives a unique list.

commonMistakes: Using {} to create an empty set — this creates an empty dictionary. Always use set() for an empty set.
Using a mutable object like a list as a dictionary key — this raises a TypeError because keys must be immutable.
Accessing a dictionary key that does not exist with dict[key] instead of dict.get(key), causing an unexpected KeyError that crashes the program.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly creates an empty set in Python?
questions.explanation: Writing {} creates an empty dictionary, not a set. The only way to create an empty set is set().
dict.get(key, default) returns the default value when the key is not found. Since 'z' is not in d, it returns 0.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can be used as a dictionary key?
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be immutable. A tuple is immutable and therefore a valid key. Lists and dictionaries are mutable and cannot be used as keys.

questions.prompt: What does the set operation A & B return?
options: All elements from A and B combined
Elements common to both A and B
Elements in A that are not in B
questions.explanation: The & operator on sets computes the intersection, which contains only the elements that appear in both sets.
The set removes duplicate values. The unique elements are {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9}, which gives a length of 7.

questions.prompt: Which method would you use to loop over both keys and values of a dictionary at the same time?
questions.explanation: dict.items() returns each entry as a (key, value) tuple, allowing you to unpack both in a for loop. dict.pairs() does not exist.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between using dict['key'] and dict.get('key') to access a value in a dictionary.
questions.answer: Using dict['key'] raises a KeyError if the key does not exist, which will crash the program. Using dict.get('key') returns None by default, or a custom default value if provided, so it is safer when you are not sure whether a key is present.
questions.explanation: Understanding this difference is important for writing robust programs that do not crash on missing data.

questions.prompt: Why are sets useful for removing duplicates from a list? Give a brief example.
questions.answer: Sets automatically discard duplicate elements because every element in a set must be unique. For example, if you have a list like [1, 2, 2, 3, 3], converting it with list(set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3])) gives [1, 2, 3] with all duplicates removed.
questions.explanation: This is a very common and practical use-case of sets — cleaning data by removing repeated values quickly.
The union of {10, 20, 30} and {20, 30, 40} is {10, 20, 30, 40}, which has 4 unique elements, so len() returns 4.

questions.prompt: Write a Python program that takes a dictionary of student names and their marks, then prints only the names of students who scored more than 75.
questions.starter:
# Dictionary of student marks
students = {
    'Aarav': 82,
    'Bhavna': 67,
    'Chirag': 91,
    'Divya': 74,
    'Esha': 88

# Write your code below
questions.explanation: We use dict.items() to loop over each name-marks pair. Inside the loop, we check if marks is greater than 75 and print the name if the condition is true. The output will be Aarav, Chirag, and Esha.

steps.say: Hello everyone! Today we are going to learn about two very useful data structures in Python — dictionaries and sets. These tools help you store and organise data in smart ways.
Think of a dictionary like a real-life contact book. Each contact has a name — that is the key — and a phone number — that is the value.
A set is like a bag where every item is unique. If you try to put a duplicate item in, it simply ignores it.
Let us create a dictionary for a student. We use curly braces, and separate each key and value with a colon.
We add the name and marks as key-value pairs, then close the braces.
To read a value, we write the dictionary name followed by the key in square brackets. We can also use dot-get for a safer lookup.
To add a new key called grade, we simply assign a value to it. Python adds it to the dictionary automatically.
The items method lets us loop over a dictionary and get both the key and value together in each step of the loop.
Inside the loop, we print both the key and its value on one line.
To remove a key from a dictionary, we use the pop method and pass the key name we want to delete.
Now let us look at sets. We create one using curly braces but without key-value pairs. Notice we added the name Priya twice.
When we print the set, Python keeps only one copy of Priya. Duplicates are removed automatically.
We can perform set operations. The pipe symbol gives the union, which combines both sets. The ampersand gives the intersection, which is only the common elements.
Union gives all unique elements from both sets, and intersection gives only the ones that appear in both.
Let us quickly recap what we learned today. A dictionary stores key-value pairs, and the keys must be unique and immutable.
A set stores only unique elements and supports union, intersection, and difference operations.
Remember — to create an empty set always use set(), because empty curly braces create a dictionary, not a set.
Great work today! Practice by creating your own dictionary and set, and try out the different methods we covered. See you in the next lesson!

lesson.summary: File handling in Python allows programs to create, read, write, and close files stored on disk using built-in functions like open(), read(), write(), and close().
shortNotes: Use open(filename, mode) to open a file; common modes are 'r' (read), 'w' (write), 'a' (append), and 'r+' (read and write).
Always close a file after use with file.close(), or use a with block which closes it automatically.
The read() method reads the entire file as one string; readline() reads one line; readlines() returns a list of all lines.
The write() method writes a string to a file; it does not add a newline automatically — you must add '\n' yourself.
Opening a file in 'w' mode erases existing content; use 'a' mode to add content without deleting what is already there.
The with statement (context manager) is the recommended way to handle files as it handles closing even if an error occurs.

detailed.explanation:
File handling means reading data from files and writing data to files stored on your computer's disk. This is important because data stored in variables is lost when a program ends, but data in files stays permanently. Python makes file handling simple with its built-in `open()` function.

To open a file, you call `open(filename, mode)`. The `filename` is a string like `'data.txt'`, and the `mode` tells Python what you want to do with the file. The most common modes are `'r'` for reading, `'w'` for writing (creates the file or overwrites it), `'a'` for appending (adds to the end without deleting), and `'r+'` for both reading and writing.

Once a file is open, you can read its contents using `read()` (entire file as one string), `readline()` (one line at a time), or `readlines()` (all lines as a list). To write to a file, use the `write()` method passing a string. Remember that `write()` does not automatically add a newline character, so you must include `'\n'` yourself when needed.

The safest and most recommended way to work with files is using the `with` statement. When you write `with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:`, Python automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error occurs inside the block. This prevents resource leaks and is considered best practice.

Always be careful about file modes: using `'w'` on an existing file will delete all its previous content immediately. If you want to keep existing content and just add more, use `'a'` (append) mode instead.

definitions.meaning: A named location on disk used to store data permanently.
A built-in Python function that opens a file and returns a file object for reading or writing.
A string argument passed to open() that specifies how the file will be used, such as 'r' for read or 'w' for write.
A method that reads the entire content of an open file and returns it as a single string.
A method that writes a given string to an open file.
A method that closes the file object and releases the system resource associated with it.
A Python construct (context manager) that automatically closes a file when the indented block finishes, even if an error occurs.
A file mode that opens an existing file and adds new content at the end without deleting existing content.

points: The syntax for opening a file is: file_object = open('filename.txt', 'mode') — remember both arguments.
Using 'w' mode creates the file if it does not exist, but destroys existing content if it does — be careful!
The with statement is preferred over manually calling close() because it is safer and cleaner.
readlines() returns a list where each element is one line of the file including the '\n' character.
To read a file line by line efficiently, use a for loop: for line in file: — this works on the file object directly.
Binary files (images, PDFs) should be opened with 'rb' or 'wb' modes, not plain 'r' or 'w'.
If you try to open a file in 'r' mode and the file does not exist, Python raises a FileNotFoundError.
Exam tip: Know the difference between read(), readline(), and readlines() — a common MCQ topic.

codeExample.code:
# File Handling in Python - Complete Example

# Step 1: Writing to a file
with open('students.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Alice\n')
    f.write('Bob\n')
    f.write('Charlie\n')
print('File written successfully.')

# Step 2: Appending to the file
with open('students.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('Diana\n')
print('Data appended successfully.')

# Step 3: Reading the entire file
with open('students.txt', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()
print('Full file content:')
print(content)

# Step 4: Reading line by line
print('Reading line by line:')
with open('students.txt', 'r') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

# Step 5: Reading all lines into a list
with open('students.txt', 'r') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print('Total students:', len(lines))
codeExample.explanation:
Line 4: 'with open' opens students.txt in write mode ('w') and names the file object 'f'. If the file exists, it is overwritten.
Lines 5-7: f.write() writes each student name followed by '\n' (newline). Without '\n', all names would appear on one line.
Line 8: The with block ends here — Python closes the file automatically.
Line 11: We reopen the same file in append mode ('a') so existing content is preserved.
Line 12: Diana is added at the end of the file without deleting Alice, Bob, or Charlie.
Line 16: We open the file in read mode ('r') and use f.read() to get the entire content as one string stored in 'content'.
Lines 18-19: We print the full content of the file.
Line 22: We loop directly over the file object 'f' — Python reads one line per iteration.
Line 23: line.strip() removes the trailing newline character '\n' so the output looks clean.
Line 26: readlines() reads all lines at once and returns a Python list. Each element is one line including '\n'.
Line 28: len(lines) gives us the total count of students (lines) in the file.

commonMistakes: Opening a file in 'w' mode when you meant 'a' mode — this silently deletes all existing content in the file with no warning.
Forgetting to add '\n' at the end of each string passed to write(), causing all written data to appear on a single line when the file is read back.
Not closing the file (or not using a with block) — this can lead to data not being saved (write buffer not flushed) or the file remaining locked.

questions.prompt: Which file mode in Python opens a file for writing and erases all existing content?
questions.explanation: 'w' (write) mode opens the file for writing. If the file already exists, its content is completely erased. 'a' appends without erasing, 'r' is read-only, and 'r+' reads and writes without erasing.

questions.prompt: What does the readlines() method return?
options: A single string containing the entire file content
The first line of the file as a string
A list of strings where each string is one line of the file
An integer representing the number of lines in the file
questions.explanation: readlines() reads all lines from the file and returns them as a Python list. Each element in the list is one line, including the newline character '\n' at the end.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of using the 'with' statement when handling files?
options: It automatically closes the file even if an error occurs
It allows reading and writing at the same time
It creates a backup of the file before opening
questions.explanation: The with statement uses Python's context manager protocol to guarantee that the file is closed when the block exits, whether normally or due to an exception. This prevents resource leaks.

questions.prompt: Which exception does Python raise when you try to open a non-existent file in read mode?
questions.explanation: Python raises FileNotFoundError when open() is called in 'r' mode and the specified file does not exist on disk. This is a subclass of OSError.

questions.prompt: You want to add new data to an existing file without deleting its current content. Which mode should you use?
questions.explanation: 'a' (append) mode opens the file and positions the write pointer at the end of the existing content, so new data is added after what is already there. 'w' would erase everything first.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly reads one single line from an open file object named 'f'?
questions.explanation: readline() reads and returns one line from the file as a string, including the trailing newline character. read() reads the entire file, readlines() returns all lines as a list, and readone() does not exist.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between 'w' mode and 'a' mode when opening a file in Python.
questions.answer: 'w' (write) mode opens a file for writing and completely erases any existing content before writing. 'a' (append) mode also opens a file for writing, but it preserves the existing content and adds new data at the end of the file.
questions.explanation: This is a very commonly tested concept. The key difference is what happens to existing content: 'w' destroys it, 'a' keeps it and adds to the end.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to close a file after you are done working with it in Python?
questions.answer: Closing a file releases the system resource (file handle) back to the operating system. It also ensures that any data written to the file is flushed from the buffer and actually saved to disk. Not closing a file can cause data loss or prevent other programs from accessing the file.
questions.explanation: File objects use OS-level resources. Leaving files open wastes resources and risks incomplete writes because data may sit in a memory buffer and never reach the disk.

questions.prompt:
Consider the following Python code. What is the exact output printed to the screen?

with open('test.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Hello\n')
    f.write('World\n')

with open('test.txt', 'r') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print(len(lines))
questions.explanation: Two strings are written to the file, each ending with a newline character. readlines() reads each line as a separate element in a list. So lines has 2 elements: 'Hello\n' and 'World\n'. len(lines) is therefore 2.

questions.prompt: Write a Python program that asks the user to enter their name and age, then saves this information to a file called 'user_info.txt' in the format 'Name: <name>, Age: <age>'. After saving, read the file and print its content to confirm.
questions.starter:

age = input('Enter your age: ')

# Write to file
# YOUR CODE HERE

# Read and print file content
# YOUR CODE HERE
questions.solution:

name = input('Enter your name: ')

# Write to file
with open('user_info.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Name: ' + name + ', Age: ' + age + '\n')

questions.explanation: We use input() to collect the user's name and age as strings. We open 'user_info.txt' in 'w' mode using a with block, then use write() to save the formatted string including a newline at the end. We then open the same file in 'r' mode, use read() to get all the content as a string, and print it to verify the data was saved correctly.

steps.say: Welcome everyone! Today we are going to learn about file handling in Python. This is a very useful topic because it lets your program save data permanently.
When your program ends, all variables are lost. But if you save data to a file on disk, it stays there even after the program closes.
Files on disk are permanent. Python makes it very easy to create, read, and write files using just a few built-in tools.

scenes.title: Opening a File and File Modes

steps.say: To work with a file in Python, you first need to open it using the built-in open function. It takes two arguments: the file name and the mode.
The mode tells Python what you want to do. Use r for reading, w for writing, and a for appending.
Write mode with w creates the file if it does not exist, but warning — it will erase all content if the file already exists.
Append mode with a is safe to use when you want to add new data without deleting what is already there.
The best way to handle files is using the with statement. It automatically closes the file for you when the block is done.
Here we open a file called notes dot txt in write mode. The file object is called f.
Inside the block we call f dot write to save a line of text. We add backslash n for a new line.
Now to read it back, we open the same file in read mode and call f dot read to get all the content as one string.

write.content:
with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data)

steps.say: Python gives you three ways to read a file and it is important to know the difference between them.
f dot read returns the entire file as one single string. Use this when the file is small.
f dot readline reads just one line each time you call it. Good when you want to process one line at a time.

write.content: readline()  -> one line as a string

steps.say: f dot readlines reads all lines and gives you a Python list where each item is one line. You can then use len to count the lines.

write.content: readlines() -> all lines as a list

steps.say: Great work today! Let us quickly recap what we learned about file handling in Python.
Use open with the file name and a mode. The three key modes are r, w, and a.
Always use the with statement so the file closes automatically and safely.
Remember that write mode will delete existing content, so use append mode if you want to keep it. And always add backslash n when you need a new line.

lesson.summary: A class is a blueprint for creating objects that bundle data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) together in Python.
shortNotes: A class is defined using the `class` keyword followed by the class name and a colon.
An object is an instance of a class created by calling the class like a function.
The `__init__` method is the constructor — it runs automatically when an object is created.
`self` refers to the current object and must be the first parameter of every instance method.
Attributes store data about an object; methods define what the object can do.
Multiple objects can be created from the same class, each with its own independent data.

detailed.explanation:
A **class** is like a blueprint or a template. Just as an architect's blueprint describes how to build a house, a class describes how to create objects. The class defines what data each object will hold (called **attributes**) and what actions each object can perform (called **methods**).

An **object** is a real, usable instance built from that blueprint. You can create many objects from one class, just like you can build many houses from one blueprint. Each object gets its own copy of the attributes, so changing one object does not affect another.

The special method `__init__` (short for initialise) acts as the **constructor**. Python calls it automatically every time you create a new object. Inside `__init__` you set up the initial values of the attributes using `self.attribute_name = value`.

The keyword `self` is a reference to the object that is being used at that moment. Every instance method must have `self` as its first parameter, even though you do not pass it manually when calling the method — Python passes it for you.

To access an attribute or call a method on an object, use **dot notation**: `object_name.attribute` or `object_name.method()`. This is the standard way to interact with objects in Python and is used everywhere in real-world Python programming.

definitions.meaning: A user-defined blueprint that bundles attributes and methods together to describe a type of object.
A specific instance created from a class, with its own set of attribute values.
The constructor method in Python that is called automatically when a new object is created.
A reference to the current instance of the class, used inside methods to access the object's own attributes and methods.
A variable that belongs to an object and stores information about it.
A function defined inside a class that describes a behaviour or action of the object.
The process of creating an object from a class by calling the class name like a function.
The syntax object.attribute or object.method() used to access members of an object.

points: The class name should follow PascalCase convention in Python — e.g., `StudentRecord`, not `studentRecord`.
Every instance method's first parameter must be `self`; forgetting it causes a TypeError.
`__init__` is not called manually; Python calls it automatically during object creation.
You can create as many objects from one class as needed, and each object has independent attribute values.
Attributes set inside `__init__` using `self.` are called instance attributes and belong to each object separately.
A method is called on an object using `obj.method()` — Python automatically passes the object as `self`.
Use `type(object)` to check which class an object belongs to — useful for debugging.
In exams, tracing what `self.attribute` holds after a series of method calls is a common question type.

codeExample.code:
# Class definition
class Student:
    # Constructor method
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name      # instance attribute
        self.marks = marks    # instance attribute

    # Method to display student info
    def display(self):
        print("Name :", self.name)
        print("Marks:", self.marks)

    # Method to check pass or fail
    def result(self):
        if self.marks >= 40:
            print(self.name, "has PASSED")
        else:
            print(self.name, "has FAILED")

# Creating objects (instances)
s1 = Student("Ananya", 85)
s2 = Student("Rohan", 32)

# Calling methods on each object
s1.display()
s1.result()

print()  # blank line for readability

s2.display()
s2.result()
codeExample.explanation:
Line 2: Define a class named Student using the class keyword.
Line 4: __init__ is the constructor; it runs when a new Student object is created. It takes self, name, and marks as parameters.
Line 5-6: self.name and self.marks are instance attributes that store each student's own data.
Line 9-11: The display method prints the student's name and marks. self gives access to the object's own attributes.
Line 14-18: The result method checks if marks are 40 or above and prints pass or fail accordingly.
Line 21: s1 = Student('Ananya', 85) creates the first object. Python calls __init__ automatically with name='Ananya' and marks=85.
Line 22: s2 = Student('Rohan', 32) creates a second, independent object with different data.
Lines 25-26: Calling s1.display() and s1.result() works on Ananya's data only.
Lines 30-31: Calling s2.display() and s2.result() works on Rohan's data only, showing that each object is independent.

commonMistakes: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of a method — this causes a TypeError saying the method received the wrong number of arguments.
Writing `__init__` incorrectly (e.g., `_init_` with single underscores) — Python will not treat it as a constructor and the attributes will not be initialised.

Trying to access an attribute without `self` inside a method (e.g., writing `name` instead of `self.name`) — this raises a NameError because Python looks for a local variable, not the object's attribute.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used to define a class in Python?
questions.explanation: The `class` keyword is used to define a class in Python, followed by the class name and a colon.

questions.prompt: What is the role of `__init__` in a Python class?
options: It deletes the object when it is no longer needed.
It is called automatically when a new object is created to initialise its attributes.
It prints the object's details to the screen.
It is used to define class-level constants.
questions.explanation: `__init__` is the constructor method. Python calls it automatically at the moment of object creation to set up the object's initial attributes.

questions.prompt: What does `self` represent inside a class method?
options: The previous object that was created
The current instance (object) on which the method is called
A global variable shared by all objects
questions.explanation: `self` is a reference to the specific object on which the method is being called, allowing access to that object's own attributes and methods.

questions.prompt: Given `class Car:` with `__init__(self, brand)` setting `self.brand = brand`, which line correctly creates an object?
questions.explanation: To create an object you call the class name like a function and pass the required arguments. Python automatically handles calling `__init__`.

questions.prompt: Two objects `a = Dog('Tommy')` and `b = Dog('Bruno')` are created from the same class. If you change `a.name = 'Max'`, what happens to `b.name`?
questions.explanation: Each object has its own independent copy of instance attributes. Changing one object's attribute does not affect another object.

questions.prompt: Which of the following will correctly call the method `greet` on an object `p` of class `Person`?
questions.explanation: Dot notation is used to call a method on an object: `object_name.method()`. Python automatically passes the object as `self`.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a class and an object in Python with a real-life analogy.
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the structure and behaviour, while an object is a real instance built from that blueprint. For example, a class is like the blueprint of a mobile phone, and each actual phone manufactured is an object — each phone has its own colour and storage, just as each object has its own attribute values.
questions.explanation: This question tests conceptual understanding. A good answer uses an analogy and mentions that many objects can be created from one class, each with independent data.

questions.prompt: Why must `self` be the first parameter in every instance method, and what happens if you forget it?
questions.answer: Python automatically passes the calling object as the first argument to every instance method, so `self` must be there to receive it. If you forget `self`, Python still passes the object, but the method has no parameter to receive it, resulting in a TypeError stating the method received too many arguments.
questions.explanation: Understanding why `self` is required — because Python passes the object implicitly — is a key conceptual point often tested in exams.
The object b is created with size=7. Calling b.show() executes print(self.size * 2) which is print(7 * 2) = print(14), so the output is 14.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class called `Rectangle` that has attributes `length` and `width`. Include a method called `area` that returns the area of the rectangle, and a method called `perimeter` that returns the perimeter. Create one object with length 8 and width 5, then print both the area and the perimeter.
questions.explanation: The `__init__` method stores length and width as instance attributes. The `area` method returns length times width. The `perimeter` method returns 2 times the sum of length and width. An object r is created with length=8 and width=5, giving area=40 and perimeter=26.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are going to learn about classes and objects in Python. Think of a class as a blueprint — just like an architect's plan for a building.
The blueprint itself is not a building. It just describes what the building will look like. Similarly a class describes what an object will look like.
When we actually build a house using that blueprint, that house is the object. We can build many houses from one blueprint.
Let us write a simple class in Python. We use the class keyword followed by the class name. Notice the name starts with a capital letter — that is the convention.
Inside the class we write the init method. This is the constructor. Python calls it automatically whenever we create a new object.
Inside init we set the attributes. Self dot name stores the name for this specific object. Self always refers to the object being created.
Now let us add a method called display. A method is just a function inside a class. It must have self as its first parameter.
To create an object we call the class name like a function and pass the required values. Here we create a student named Ananya with 85 marks.
We call the display method on s1 using dot notation. Python automatically passes s1 as self, so we do not write it ourselves.
We can create as many objects as we want from the same class. Let us create a second student named Rohan with 32 marks.
Each object has its own data. Changing s1 dot marks will not affect s2 at all. They are completely independent from each other.
This is the power of object oriented programming — one class, many independent objects, each managing its own information.
Great work! Let us quickly recap what we covered today. A class is a blueprint defined with the class keyword.
The init method is the constructor that sets up attributes when an object is created. Self always refers to the current object.
We create objects by calling the class like a function, and we use dot notation to access attributes and call methods. You are ready to write your own classes!
