topics.title: What is Java and How the JVM Works

lesson.summary: Java is a platform-independent, object-oriented programming language that compiles source code into bytecode, which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) then interprets and runs on any operating system.
shortNotes: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and released in 1995.
Java source files (.java) are compiled by javac into bytecode (.class files), not into machine code directly.
The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) reads bytecode and translates it into machine-specific instructions at runtime.
Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA) means the same .class file runs on Windows, Linux, or macOS without changes.
The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) includes the JVM plus standard libraries; the JDK (Java Development Kit) includes the JRE plus the compiler and developer tools.
Java is strongly typed, meaning every variable must have a declared data type before use.

detailed.explanation:
Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle) and officially released in 1995. Java is one of the most widely used languages in the world, powering Android apps, enterprise web applications, and much more.

When you write a Java program, you save it as a `.java` file. The Java compiler (`javac`) then compiles this source code into **bytecode**, which is stored in a `.class` file. Bytecode is not machine code — it is an intermediate, platform-neutral instruction set that no physical processor understands directly.

This is where the **JVM (Java Virtual Machine)** comes in. The JVM is a software engine installed on your computer that reads the `.class` bytecode file and translates each instruction into the native machine code of your specific operating system and hardware. Because every major platform has its own JVM implementation, the same `.class` file runs everywhere — this is the famous **Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA)** principle.

The three key components to understand are: the **JDK** (Java Development Kit), which you install when you want to write and compile Java programs; the **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment), which contains the JVM and standard libraries needed to run programs; and the **JVM** itself, which is the engine that executes bytecode. The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM.

The JVM also handles important tasks like memory management through **Garbage Collection**, security checks, and just-in-time (JIT) compilation, where frequently executed bytecode is compiled directly to machine code for better performance.

definitions.meaning: A high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent programming language created by Sun Microsystems in 1995.
A software engine that executes Java bytecode by translating it into machine-specific instructions at runtime.
An intermediate, platform-neutral code generated by the Java compiler from .java source files, stored in .class files.
A full software package that includes the Java compiler (javac), JRE, and other developer tools needed to write and compile Java programs.
A subset of the JDK that includes the JVM and standard class libraries required to run Java programs but not to compile them.
Java's principle that compiled bytecode can run on any device or OS that has a compatible JVM installed, without recompilation.
An automatic memory management process in the JVM that frees memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use.
A component of the JVM that compiles frequently used bytecode into native machine code at runtime to improve performance.

points: Java source code (.java) → compiled by javac → bytecode (.class) → executed by JVM: remember this flow for exams.
The JVM is platform-specific (there is a different JVM for Windows, Linux, Mac), but the bytecode is platform-independent.
JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM. You need JDK to develop; JRE alone is enough to run.
Java is NOT compiled directly to machine code (unlike C or C++); this is what gives it platform independence.
The main class in a Java program must have the method: public static void main(String[] args) — this is the entry point.
Java is case-sensitive: 'Hello' and 'hello' are treated as different identifiers.
Garbage Collection happens automatically in Java; you do not need to manually free memory like in C.
The JIT compiler improves performance by converting hot (frequently run) bytecode into native machine code during execution.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1-3: Comments explaining the file name and purpose. Java ignores these lines.
Line 5: We declare a public class named HelloJava. The file name must match the class name exactly.
Line 8: The main method — public static void main(String[] args) — is the entry point the JVM calls first when running the program.
Line 11: System.out.println prints a line of text to the console and moves to the next line.
Line 14: System.getProperty("java.version") asks the JVM for the current Java version at runtime; this shows that the JVM knows its environment.
Line 15: We print the version string with a label using the + operator to join strings.
Line 18-19: Similarly, os.name gives the operating system name, demonstrating WORA — the same bytecode prints a different OS name depending on where it runs.

commonMistakes: Naming the file differently from the public class name — for example, saving a class named 'HelloJava' in a file called 'hello.java' causes a compilation error because Java requires the file name and public class name to match exactly.

Confusing JDK, JRE, and JVM — students often think installing any one of them is enough for both writing and running programs; remember that to compile and run you need the JDK, while just running requires the JRE.

Thinking Java bytecode is machine code — bytecode is an intermediate format understood only by the JVM, not directly by your computer's processor; this misunderstanding causes confusion about why Java needs the JVM installed.

questions.prompt: What does the Java compiler (javac) produce when it compiles a .java source file?
questions.explanation: The javac compiler converts Java source code (.java) into bytecode stored in a .class file. This bytecode is platform-independent and is later interpreted by the JVM.

questions.prompt: Which component of the Java ecosystem is responsible for executing Java bytecode?
questions.explanation: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) reads the .class bytecode file and translates its instructions into native machine code for the host operating system.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym WORA stand for in the context of Java?
questions.explanation: WORA — Write Once, Run Anywhere — means that Java bytecode compiled on one platform can run on any other platform that has a compatible JVM, without needing to recompile.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
options: JVM contains JRE which contains JDK
JRE contains JDK which contains JVM
JDK contains JRE which contains JVM
They are three separate, unrelated tools
questions.explanation: JDK is the largest package: it includes the JRE (plus compiler and tools). The JRE includes the JVM (plus standard libraries). So JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct entry point method signature that the JVM looks for to start a Java application?
questions.explanation: The JVM requires the method to be exactly: public static void main(String[] args). It must be public (accessible), static (no object needed), void (returns nothing), and take a String array as parameter.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler inside the JVM?
options: It compiles .java files into .class files before execution
It converts frequently used bytecode into native machine code at runtime for better performance
It automatically writes Java source code from requirements
It compresses .class files to save disk space
questions.explanation: The JIT compiler is a part of the JVM that identifies frequently executed bytecode (hot code) and compiles it into native machine code during runtime, speeding up execution significantly.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words why Java is called a platform-independent language.
questions.answer: Java is platform-independent because the Java compiler converts source code into bytecode, which is not tied to any specific operating system or hardware. The JVM installed on each platform then translates this bytecode into the local machine's native instructions, so the same bytecode runs on Windows, Linux, or macOS without modification.
questions.explanation: The key insight is that it is the bytecode (not the source code) that travels across platforms, and each platform's JVM handles the translation to native machine code.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the JRE and the JDK? Which one should a student install to write and run Java programs?
questions.answer: The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) contains the JVM and standard libraries — it is only for running Java programs. The JDK (Java Development Kit) contains everything in the JRE plus the compiler (javac) and other developer tools. A student who wants to write and compile Java programs must install the JDK.
questions.explanation: End users who only need to run Java apps install the JRE. Developers must install the JDK because it includes the compiler needed to turn source code into bytecode.

questions.answer:
Java
1995
questions.explanation: System.out.println prints each argument on its own line. The first call prints the string Java and the second prints the integer 1995, each followed by a newline.

questions.prompt:
Write a Java program that prints the following three lines exactly:
Welcome to Java
Platform: Independent
Powered by JVM
questions.explanation: Each System.out.println() call prints one line of text to the console and automatically moves to the next line. The string argument passed inside the parentheses and double quotes is printed exactly as written. Three separate println calls produce three separate output lines.

steps.say: Hello everyone, welcome to your very first Java lesson. Today we are going to answer two big questions: what is Java, and how does it actually run on your computer?

write.content: What is Java and How the JVM Works

steps.say: Java is a programming language created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems, and it was released in 1995. Today it powers everything from Android apps to large banking systems.
The most important feature of Java is that it is platform-independent, meaning code you write today can run on Windows, Linux, or Mac without any changes.
When you write a Java program, you save it as a dot-java file. Let us trace what happens next, step by step.
You then run the Java compiler, called javac, on that file. The compiler reads your source code and produces a dot-class file.
The dot-class file contains something called bytecode. Bytecode is not machine code — it is a special in-between language that no processor understands directly.
Think of bytecode as a universal language that every machine agrees to understand through a helper called the JVM.

scenes.title: The JVM – The Heart of Java

steps.say: Now here is the magic. Each operating system has its own version of the JVM, the Java Virtual Machine. It reads the bytecode and translates it into instructions your specific machine understands.
So the same dot-class file that runs on your Windows laptop also runs on your friend's Linux machine, because each has its own JVM that handles the translation.
This is the famous Write Once Run Anywhere principle. You write and compile once, and the JVM on each platform does the rest.
Students often get confused between three terms: JDK, JRE, and JVM. Let me draw this clearly for you.
The JVM is the engine that runs bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries Java programs need.
The JDK is the full development kit. It includes the JRE plus the compiler and tools. As a student writing programs, always install the JDK.
Let us look at the simplest Java program so you can see the structure the JVM expects.
Every Java program needs a main method. This is the entry point — the first thing the JVM calls when it runs your program.
Inside main, we call System dot out dot println to print a message to the screen. Then we close both braces.
Great work today! Let us quickly recap what we learned.
Java source code is compiled by javac into bytecode, stored in a dot-class file.
The JVM on each platform reads that bytecode and runs it, giving us platform independence.

write.content: JVM runs bytecode on any platform

steps.say: And remember: install the JDK to develop, the JRE alone is only for running. See you in the next lesson!

lesson.summary: A Java program has a fixed structure built around a class definition, a main method, and statements — understanding this skeleton is the first step to writing any Java program.
shortNotes: Every Java program must have at least one class defined using the `class` keyword.
Execution always starts from the `main` method with the exact signature: `public static void main(String[] args)`.
Curly braces `{}` mark the beginning and end of every class and method body.
Java is case-sensitive — `Main`, `main`, and `MAIN` are three different identifiers.
Each statement in Java ends with a semicolon `;`.
The file name must exactly match the public class name, with the `.java` extension.

detailed.explanation:
A Java program is organized around **classes**. Even the simplest program must be written inside a class. You define a class using the keyword `class` followed by the class name and a pair of curly braces `{}`. Everything that belongs to the class lives inside those braces.

Inside the class, you write **methods** — blocks of code that perform tasks. The most important method is `main`. When you run a Java program, the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) looks for a method with the exact signature `public static void main(String[] args)` and starts executing from the first line inside it. If this signature is even slightly wrong, the program will not run.

Statements are the individual instructions inside a method. In Java, every statement must end with a **semicolon** `;`. For example, `System.out.println("Hello");` is a single statement that prints a line of text to the screen. Forgetting the semicolon is one of the most common beginner errors.

The **file name** must match the name of the `public` class exactly, including the capitalisation. For example, if your class is named `HelloWorld`, the file must be saved as `HelloWorld.java`. After compiling with `javac HelloWorld.java`, a file named `HelloWorld.class` is created, which the JVM then runs using `java HelloWorld`.

Overall, the skeleton of a Java program is: a class declaration wrapping a `main` method, which in turn contains statements. Mastering this structure is the foundation for everything else in Java.

definitions.meaning: A blueprint or container in Java that holds data and methods; every Java program must have at least one class.
A named block of code inside a class that performs a specific task when called.
The special method `public static void main(String[] args)` where program execution begins.
A single instruction in Java that ends with a semicolon, e.g., a print or assignment instruction.
The engine that runs compiled Java bytecode (.class files) on any platform.
The set of rules that define how Java code must be written so the compiler can understand it.
A name given to a class, method, or variable by the programmer; Java identifiers are case-sensitive.

points: The `main` method signature must be exactly `public static void main(String[] args)` — changing any word will prevent execution.
Java is strictly case-sensitive: `system.out.println` will not work; only `System.out.println` is correct.
Every opening brace `{` must have a matching closing brace `}` — mismatched braces cause compile errors.
The public class name and the file name must be identical, including capitalisation.
A program can have many classes in one file, but only one class can be declared `public`, and it must match the file name.
Statements inside methods end with `;`; class and method declarations end with `{}`, not `;`.
The `System.out.println()` method prints text followed by a newline; `System.out.print()` prints without a newline.
Compilation converts `.java` source code to `.class` bytecode; running executes the bytecode on the JVM.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: A single-line comment using `//`; comments are ignored by the compiler and are just notes for the reader.
Line 2: `public class HelloWorld` — declares a public class named HelloWorld; the opening `{` starts the class body.
Line 5: `public static void main(String[] args)` — the main method declaration; this is the entry point of the program.
Line 8: `System.out.println("Hello, World!");` — a statement that prints the text Hello, World! followed by a newline; ends with `;`.
Line 11: A second print statement that outputs Welcome to Java! on a new line.
Line 13: `}` closes the main method body.
Line 15: `}` closes the class body.

commonMistakes: Writing `public static void Main(String[] args)` with a capital M — Java is case-sensitive and will not find the entry point, causing a runtime error.
Saving the file as `helloworld.java` when the class is named `HelloWorld` — the file name must exactly match the public class name in capitalisation.
Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement, e.g., writing `System.out.println("Hi")` without `;` — this causes a compile-time error.

questions.prompt: Where does execution of a Java program always begin?
options: The first class defined in the file
The `public static void main(String[] args)` method
The first variable declaration in the program
Any method marked with the `start` keyword
questions.explanation: The JVM always looks for the exact method signature `public static void main(String[] args)` as the entry point. There is no `start` keyword in Java.

questions.prompt: If a public class is named `StudentInfo`, what must the file be saved as?
questions.explanation: The file name must exactly match the public class name including capitalisation, and must use the `.java` extension. The `.class` file is produced after compilation, not written by the programmer.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly ends a Java statement?
questions.explanation: In Java, every statement must end with a semicolon `;`. Forgetting it is one of the most common compile-time errors.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of curly braces `{}` in a Java program?
options: They mark the end of a statement
They are used only for comments
They define the beginning and end of a class or method body
They are optional decorators with no effect
questions.explanation: Curly braces delimit code blocks. Every class body and every method body must be enclosed in a matching pair of `{}`.

questions.prompt: Which command compiles a Java source file named `Demo.java`?
questions.explanation: `javac` is the Java compiler. It takes a `.java` source file and produces a `.class` bytecode file. The `java` command is used to run the compiled bytecode.

questions.prompt: How many `public` classes can be defined in a single Java source file?
options: None — public classes are not allowed in source files
questions.explanation: A Java source file can contain multiple classes, but only one of them may be declared `public`, and the file name must match that public class's name.

questions.prompt: Explain why the `main` method in Java is declared as `public static void`. What does each keyword mean in this context?
questions.answer: `public` means the method is accessible from anywhere, including by the JVM. `static` means the method belongs to the class itself, so the JVM can call it without creating an object of the class. `void` means the method does not return any value.
questions.explanation: Each modifier in the main method signature serves a specific purpose: accessibility, the ability to call without an instance, and indicating no return value.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `System.out.println()` and `System.out.print()` in Java?
questions.answer: `System.out.println()` prints the given text and then moves the cursor to a new line, so the next output appears on the next line. `System.out.print()` prints the text but does not add a newline at the end, so the next output continues on the same line.
questions.explanation: Understanding the difference helps beginners control the formatting of their program output.

`println("Line 1")` outputs Line 1 and moves to a new line. `print("Line 2")` outputs Line 2 without a newline. `println(" and Line 3")` outputs and Line 3 on the same line as Line 2 and then moves to a new line. So there are exactly 2 lines of output: 'Line 1' and 'Line 2 and Line 3'.

questions.prompt: Write a complete Java program in a class named `MyProfile` that prints your name on the first line, your college name on the second line, and your favourite subject on the third line.
questions.explanation: Three `System.out.println()` statements are used, one for each piece of information. Each call prints its argument and then moves to a new line, producing three separate lines of output. The program follows the standard Java structure: a public class whose name matches the file name, containing the main method, with statements ending in semicolons.

steps.say: Hello everyone, welcome to our Java programming course. Today we are going to look at something very fundamental — the structure of a Java program.
Think of it like a letter. A letter has a greeting, a body, and a closing. A Java program also has a fixed skeleton you must follow every single time.
Every Java program lives inside a class. You declare a class using the keyword class, followed by the class name, and then a pair of curly braces.
The opening curly brace marks the start of the class body. Everything belonging to this class goes inside these braces.
And the closing curly brace marks the end of the class. Every opening brace must have a matching closing brace.

scenes.title: The main Method — Where Execution Begins

steps.say: Inside the class, we write the main method. This is the most important method because the Java Virtual Machine always starts running your program from here.
The keywords public, static, and void each have a specific role. Public means anyone can access it, static means it belongs to the class, and void means it returns nothing.

write.content: public  static  void  — each word matters

steps.say: Now let us add a statement inside the main method. This line prints Hello World to the screen.
Notice the semicolon at the end of the statement. In Java, every statement must end with a semicolon — forgetting it is a very common mistake.
Let us now see the whole program together, from top to bottom.
The main method goes inside the class body.
Our print statement goes inside the main method.
We close the main method and then close the class with two closing braces. Also remember the file must be saved as HelloWorld dot java.
Let us quickly recap what we learned today. Every Java program must have a class, and the class name must match the file name exactly.
Execution always starts from the main method with that exact signature.
Every statement ends with a semicolon, and every block of code is wrapped in matching curly braces.
That is the foundation of every Java program you will ever write. Practice this structure until it becomes second nature. See you in the next lesson!

topics.title: Variables and Data Types in Java

lesson.summary: Variables are named memory locations that store data values, and Java provides several built-in primitive and reference data types to define what kind of data a variable can hold.
shortNotes: A variable in Java must be declared with a data type before it can be used.
Java has 8 primitive data types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean.
String is a reference data type (a class), not a primitive, but is very commonly used.
Variable names are case-sensitive and must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign.
Java is a statically typed language, meaning the type of a variable is fixed at compile time.
Use int for whole numbers, double for decimals, char for a single character, and boolean for true/false values.

detailed.explanation:
A **variable** is a named container in memory that holds a value your program can read or change. In Java, before you can use a variable, you must **declare** it by specifying its data type and giving it a name, for example `int age = 20;`. This tells the compiler to reserve the right amount of memory and to only allow integer values in that container.

Java has **8 primitive data types**. The most commonly used ones are `int` (whole numbers, 4 bytes), `double` (decimal numbers, 8 bytes), `char` (a single character, 2 bytes), and `boolean` (true or false, 1 bit logically). Less commonly used primitives include `byte`, `short`, `long`, and `float`. Each type has a specific size and range, which is important when memory efficiency matters.

**Reference data types** store the address of an object rather than the value itself. The most important example for beginners is `String`, which represents a sequence of characters, like `String name = "Rahul";`. Unlike primitives, reference types are based on classes and have methods you can call on them.

Java is a **statically typed** language. This means the data type of a variable is decided at compile time and cannot change during the program's execution. For example, if you declare `int marks = 85;`, you cannot later store a decimal number like `85.5` in the same variable without changing its type or using a cast.

You can also declare a variable without immediately assigning a value — this is called **declaration without initialization** — but you must assign a value before you use it, or the compiler will give an error. It is good practice to initialize variables when you declare them to avoid unexpected behavior.

definitions.meaning: A named memory location that stores a value of a specific data type in a Java program.
A classification that tells the compiler what kind of value a variable can hold and how much memory to allocate.
One of Java's 8 built-in basic types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean) that store simple values directly.
A data type that stores a reference (memory address) to an object rather than the value itself; examples include String and arrays.
The statement that introduces a variable to the compiler by specifying its type and name, e.g., int age;
Assigning a value to a variable for the first time, e.g., age = 20; or int age = 20;
A feature of Java where each variable's data type is checked and fixed at compile time, not at runtime.

points: Always declare a variable with its data type in Java: `int x = 5;` not just `x = 5;`.
The default value for int is 0, double is 0.0, boolean is false, and object references are null — but only for class-level (instance/static) variables, not local variables.
Use `long` instead of `int` when storing very large numbers; append L to the literal, e.g., `long population = 1400000000L;`.
Use `double` for decimal precision; avoid `float` unless memory is a constraint (float uses 4 bytes, double uses 8 bytes).
char values are enclosed in single quotes: `char grade = 'A';` while String values use double quotes: `String name = "Amit";`.
Variable names cannot start with a digit, cannot be a Java keyword (like int, class, for), and cannot contain spaces.
Java follows camelCase naming convention for variables: `studentAge`, `totalMarks`, `isEligible`.
Exam tip: Know the size of each primitive type — int is 4 bytes, long is 8 bytes, double is 8 bytes, char is 2 bytes, byte is 1 byte.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: We define a public class named VariablesDemo — every Java program needs a class.
Line 2: The main method is the entry point of the program.
Line 5: We declare an int variable 'age' and assign the value 21 — suitable for whole numbers.
Line 8: We declare a double variable 'percentage' with a decimal value 87.5.
Line 11: We declare a char variable 'grade' with the character 'A' in single quotes.
Line 14: We declare a boolean variable 'isEnrolled' set to true — only true or false allowed.
Line 17: We declare a String variable 'studentName' with a name in double quotes — String is a reference type.
Line 20: We declare a long variable 'collegeId' with a large number; the L suffix marks it as a long literal.
Lines 23-28: We use System.out.println to print each variable's value to the console, concatenating labels with the + operator.

commonMistakes: Using single quotes for String values — String must use double quotes ("Hello"), while char uses single quotes ('H'). Writing String name = 'Rahul'; is a compile error.
Forgetting to initialize a local variable before using it — Java does not give local variables a default value, so using an uninitialized local variable causes a compile-time error.
Storing a decimal number in an int variable without casting — writing int marks = 95.5; causes a compile error; you must either use double or cast: int marks = (int) 95.5;

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct way to declare an integer variable in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, the keyword for integer type is 'int' (all lowercase). 'integer' is not a keyword, 'Int' has wrong capitalization, and the type must come before the variable name.

questions.prompt: What is the size of the 'double' data type in Java?
questions.explanation: The double data type in Java occupies 8 bytes (64 bits) of memory and can store decimal numbers with double precision.

questions.prompt: Which of the following variable names is NOT valid in Java?

questions.prompt: Which data type would you use to store the value true or false in Java?
questions.explanation: The boolean data type in Java is specifically designed to hold only two values: true or false. It is commonly used in conditions and flags.

questions.prompt: What is the correct literal suffix used when assigning a value to a long variable in Java?

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about String in Java is correct?
options: String is a primitive data type in Java.
String values are enclosed in single quotes.
String is a reference data type based on a class.
String variables cannot be printed using System.out.println.
questions.explanation: String is a reference data type in Java — it is actually a class in the java.lang package. Its values are enclosed in double quotes, and it can be printed using System.out.println.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a primitive data type and a reference data type in Java? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: A primitive data type stores the actual value directly in memory (e.g., int stores the integer value itself). A reference data type stores the memory address of an object rather than the value (e.g., String stores a reference to a String object). Java has 8 primitive types, while reference types are based on classes.
questions.explanation: Understanding this distinction helps students grasp how Java manages memory and why operations on reference types (like comparing with ==) behave differently than on primitives.

questions.prompt: Why is Java called a statically typed language, and how does this affect how you write variables?
questions.answer: Java is called statically typed because the data type of every variable is checked and fixed at compile time, not at runtime. This means you must declare a variable's type before using it, and you cannot store a value of a different incompatible type in it later without explicit conversion. For example, once you declare int age = 20;, you cannot store 20.5 in age without changing the type.
questions.explanation: Static typing helps Java catch type errors early during compilation rather than at runtime, making programs more reliable.
When an int and a double are added in Java, the int is automatically promoted to double (widening conversion), and the result is a double. So 10 + 2.5 = 12.5, and System.out.println prints 12.5.

lesson.summary: Operators in Java are special symbols that perform operations on variables and values, including arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, and more.
shortNotes: Java operators are symbols that act on operands to produce a result.
Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, % for basic math calculations.
Relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= compare two values and return boolean.
Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT) combine boolean expressions.
Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, /= assign or update variable values.
Operator precedence determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression.

detailed.explanation:
An **operator** in Java is a symbol that tells the compiler to perform a specific operation on one or more operands. For example, `+` adds two numbers and `==` checks if two values are equal. Java has several categories of operators, each designed for a different purpose.

**Arithmetic operators** (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) work on numeric values. The modulus operator `%` returns the remainder of a division — for example, `10 % 3` gives `1`. Integer division truncates the decimal part, so `7 / 2` gives `3`, not `3.5`.

**Relational (comparison) operators** (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) compare two values and always return a `boolean` result (`true` or `false`). These are heavily used in `if` statements and loops. Remember: `==` checks equality, while `=` is assignment — confusing them is a very common bug.

**Logical operators** (`&&`, `||`, `!`) work on boolean values. `&&` returns `true` only if both sides are true; `||` returns `true` if at least one side is true; `!` flips the boolean value. Java uses **short-circuit evaluation**: if the first operand of `&&` is `false`, the second is not evaluated at all.

**Assignment operators** (`=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`) store values in variables. Compound operators like `x += 5` are shorthand for `x = x + 5`. Java also has **increment/decrement** operators: `++` adds 1 and `--` subtracts 1. The prefix form (`++x`) changes the value before use, while the postfix form (`x++`) changes it after use.

definitions.meaning: A symbol that performs a specific operation on one or more operands.
A value or variable on which an operator acts.
An operator that performs mathematical calculations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus.
An operator that compares two values and returns a boolean result (true or false).
An operator (&&, ||, !) that combines or inverts boolean expressions.
An operator that stores a value into a variable; compound forms like += also compute before storing.
The rule that determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression; e.g., * is evaluated before +.
A feature of && and || where the second operand is skipped if the result is already determined by the first operand.

points: Use == to compare primitive values; never use == to compare String content (use .equals() instead).
Integer division in Java drops the decimal: 7/2 gives 3. Cast to double if you need 3.5: (double)7/2.
The % operator works on integers and gives the remainder; useful for checking even/odd: n % 2 == 0 means n is even.
Operator precedence: *, /, % are evaluated before +, -. Use parentheses to make your intention clear.
Pre-increment (++x) vs post-increment (x++): the difference matters when used inside expressions.
Short-circuit evaluation in && and || can prevent runtime errors, e.g., checking for null before calling a method.
The ternary operator (condition ? valueIfTrue : valueFIfFalse) is a compact alternative to a simple if-else.
Exam tip: Always trace through expressions step by step using operator precedence to find the final value.

questions.prompt: What is the result of the expression 17 % 5 in Java?

questions.prompt: Which operator is used to check equality between two primitive values in Java?

questions.prompt: In Java, what does the expression (true && false) || (!false) evaluate to?

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between pre-increment (++x) and post-increment (x++) in Java with a brief example.
questions.answer: Pre-increment (++x) increases the value of x by 1 before the expression is evaluated, so the new value is used immediately. Post-increment (x++) uses the current value of x in the expression first, and then increases it by 1. For example, if x=5, then y=++x gives y=6 and x=6, but y=x++ gives y=5 and x=6.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is timing: when does the increment actually happen relative to the use of the variable in the expression.

questions.prompt: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java? Why is it useful?
questions.answer: Short-circuit evaluation means that in a logical AND (&&) expression, if the first operand is false, Java does not evaluate the second operand because the result is already known to be false. Similarly for OR (||), if the first operand is true, the second is skipped. This is useful for preventing errors, such as checking if an object is not null before calling a method on it.
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation is both a performance optimization and a safety mechanism when the second operand could cause an error if evaluated.

steps.say: Hello everyone, welcome to today's lesson. We are going to learn about operators in Java, which are the building blocks of every calculation and decision in your programs.
An operator is a symbol that tells Java to perform an action on one or more values. Those values are called operands.
For example, in the expression 5 plus 3, the plus sign is the operator and 5 and 3 are the operands.
Let us start with arithmetic operators. These are the ones you already know from maths, and they work just the same in Java.
We have plus for addition, minus for subtraction, star for multiplication, slash for division, and percent for remainder.
Be careful with division. If both values are integers, Java drops the decimal. So 7 divided by 2 gives 3, not 3.5.
The percent sign gives the remainder. So 10 percent 3 equals 1, because 10 divided by 3 leaves a remainder of 1.
Compound assignment operators are shortcuts. Instead of writing x equals x plus 5, you can write x plus-equals 5. They work the same way.
Next we have relational operators. These compare two values and always give you a true or false answer.
The double equals checks equality, not single equals. Single equals is always for assignment. This is one of the most common mistakes beginners make.
Now logical operators let you combine conditions. Double ampersand means AND, double pipe means OR, and exclamation mark means NOT.
AND returns true only when both sides are true. OR returns true when at least one side is true. NOT flips the boolean value.
Let us see these operators in action with a quick code example. We declare two integers a equals 15 and b equals 4.
Now we print the division and remainder. Division gives 3 because Java drops the decimal, and remainder gives 3.
We can also use a relational operator to check if a is greater than b. This prints true because 15 is indeed greater than 4.
And here is the ternary operator, which is a short way to write a simple if-else. If marks are 55 or above, result is Pass, otherwise Fail.
Great work everyone. Let us quickly recap what we learned today about operators in Java.
Arithmetic operators do maths. Remember integer division drops the decimal, and percent gives the remainder.
Relational operators compare values and return true or false. Always use double equals for comparison, not single equals.
Logical operators combine boolean values. And needs both true, Or needs just one true, and Not flips the value.
Keep practicing these with small programs and you will be very comfortable with operators in no time. See you in the next lesson!

lesson.summary: The Scanner class in Java allows programs to read input from the user through the keyboard at runtime.
shortNotes: Import Scanner using: import java.util.Scanner; at the top of the program
Create a Scanner object with: Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
Use sc.nextInt() for integers, sc.nextDouble() for decimals, sc.next() for a single word, and sc.nextLine() for a full line
Always close the Scanner after use with sc.close() to free system resources
System.in tells Scanner to read from the keyboard (standard input stream)
Scanner is part of the java.util package, so it must be imported before use

detailed.explanation:
When a Java program runs, it sometimes needs to ask the user for information — like their name, age, or marks. Java provides a built-in class called `Scanner` that makes it easy to read this input from the keyboard. It is available in the `java.util` package, so you must import it before using it.

To use Scanner, you first create an object of the class: `Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);`. Here, `System.in` is the standard input stream — it represents the keyboard. The variable `sc` is just a name you choose; you can call it anything.

Once the Scanner object is created, you can call different methods on it depending on what type of data you want to read. Use `sc.nextInt()` to read a whole number, `sc.nextDouble()` to read a decimal number, `sc.next()` to read one word (stops at a space), and `sc.nextLine()` to read an entire line of text including spaces.

A common issue beginners face is mixing `nextInt()` (or similar) with `nextLine()`. After `nextInt()` reads a number, it leaves the newline character `\n` in the input buffer. If you call `nextLine()` right after, it reads that leftover newline instead of the actual next line. The fix is to call an extra `sc.nextLine()` to consume the leftover newline before reading the string.

Always close the Scanner at the end of your program using `sc.close()`. This is good practice because it releases the resources tied to the input stream. Leaving it open is not harmful in small programs, but it is considered poor coding habit.

definitions.meaning: A class in java.util that is used to read input data (integers, strings, decimals, etc.) from various sources like the keyboard or a file.
A built-in Java object representing the standard input stream, which is usually the keyboard.
A Scanner method that reads and returns the next integer value entered by the user.
A Scanner method that reads and returns an entire line of text, including spaces, until the user presses Enter.
A Scanner method that reads and returns the next single token (word), stopping at whitespace.
A Scanner method that reads and returns the next floating-point (decimal) number entered by the user.
A line written at the top of a Java file that tells the compiler to include an external class or package for use in the program.

points: Always write import java.util.Scanner; as the very first line before the class definition.
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); — System.in means keyboard input; forgetting it is a very common error.
Match the method to the data type: nextInt() for int, nextDouble() for double, next() for String word, nextLine() for full String.
The newline-flush problem: after using nextInt() or nextDouble(), call an extra sc.nextLine() before reading a String with nextLine().
sc.close() should be called after all input reading is done — this is good practice and may be asked in exams.
Scanner can also read from files, but for basic programs System.in (keyboard) is used.
If the user enters the wrong type (e.g., a letter when an integer is expected), Java throws InputMismatchException at runtime.
You can prompt the user before reading by using System.out.print() so the cursor stays on the same line.

Using nextLine() immediately after nextInt() or nextDouble() without flushing the buffer — the leftover newline character causes nextLine() to return an empty string instead of reading the actual input.
Calling sc.nextLine() when you need only one word and wondering why it reads too much — use sc.next() for a single word and sc.nextLine() only when you need spaces in the input.

options: A file on the hard disk
questions.explanation: System.in is Java's standard input stream, which by default reads from the keyboard.

The newline character left by nextInt() is consumed by nextLine() before reading actual input
nextLine() always returns an empty string

questions.prompt: Which method is the correct one to read a decimal number such as 98.5 using Scanner?
questions.explanation: sc.nextDouble() reads a double-precision decimal value. sc.nextFloat() also exists but nextDouble() is more commonly used and precise. sc.readDouble() and sc.nextDecimal() do not exist.

questions.prompt: Explain why sc.close() is called at the end of a program that uses Scanner, and what happens if you do not call it.
questions.answer: sc.close() releases the system resources (specifically the input stream) associated with the Scanner object. If you do not call it, in small programs nothing visibly bad happens, but it is considered poor practice because it may cause resource leaks in larger applications and can also trigger IDE warnings.
questions.explanation: Closing the Scanner is about responsible resource management. The Scanner wraps System.in; closing it signals that no more input will be read and the underlying stream can be released.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between sc.next() and sc.nextLine() in the Scanner class? Give an example scenario where each is appropriate.
questions.answer: sc.next() reads one token (word) and stops at any whitespace, so it is suitable for reading a single word like a username with no spaces. sc.nextLine() reads everything until the user presses Enter, including spaces, making it suitable for reading a full name like 'Rahul Kumar' or a sentence.
questions.explanation: Understanding this difference is important to avoid reading incomplete input when spaces are expected in the data.

lesson.summary: Conditional statements in Java allow a program to make decisions and execute different blocks of code based on whether a condition is true or false.
shortNotes: if statement runs a block only when its condition is true.
if-else gives two paths: one for true, one for false.
else-if ladder checks multiple conditions one by one.
switch statement matches a variable against several fixed values (cases).
Conditions use relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=.
Logical operators && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT) combine or negate conditions.

detailed.explanation:
A **conditional statement** lets your program choose what to do based on a condition. Instead of always running the same code from top to bottom, your program can ask a question like "Is the user's age above 18?" and take different actions depending on the answer.

The simplest form is the `if` statement. You write a condition inside parentheses; if it evaluates to `true`, the block inside the curly braces runs. If it is `false`, that block is skipped entirely.

An `if-else` statement adds a second block that runs when the condition is `false`. This gives you exactly two paths. When you need more than two paths, you chain `else if` blocks together — Java checks each condition from top to bottom and runs the first one that is `true`. Any remaining `else` block acts as a default.

The `switch` statement is a cleaner alternative when you are comparing one variable against many specific constant values (like integers or characters). Each `case` label matches a possible value, and a `break` statement stops execution from falling into the next case. A `default` case handles values that do not match any label.

Choosing the right conditional structure makes code easier to read and maintain. Use `if-else` for range checks or complex boolean expressions, and prefer `switch` when matching a single variable to a list of exact values.

definitions.meaning: A boolean expression that evaluates to either true or false, used to control which code block runs.
A conditional statement that executes a block of code only when its condition is true.
A conditional structure that executes one block if the condition is true and another block if it is false.
A chain of if and else-if blocks used to test multiple conditions sequentially.
A conditional statement that compares a single variable to multiple constant case values and executes the matching block.
A keyword used inside a switch block to stop execution from continuing into the next case.
The optional last case in a switch statement that runs when no other case matches.
An operator such as ==, !=, <, or > that compares two values and returns a boolean result.

points: Always use == to compare values in conditions, not = (which is assignment).
Curly braces {} are optional for a single-statement body, but always using them prevents bugs.
In an else-if ladder, only the first matching condition executes; the rest are skipped.
switch works with byte, short, int, char, String, and enum types — not with float or double.
Forgetting break in a switch causes fall-through: execution continues into the next case.
The default case in switch does not have to be last, but placing it last is best practice.
Logical AND (&&) requires both conditions to be true; logical OR (||) requires at least one to be true.
Exam tip: Trace code step-by-step, evaluating each condition with the given values to predict output.

lesson.summary: Loops in Java allow you to repeat a block of code multiple times using for, while, and do-while constructs, making programs efficient and concise.
shortNotes: Java has three loop types: for, while, and do-while.
A for loop is best when the number of iterations is known in advance.
A while loop checks the condition before executing the body.
A do-while loop executes the body at least once before checking the condition.
Use break to exit a loop early and continue to skip the current iteration.
An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition never becomes false — always update the loop variable.

detailed.explanation:
A **loop** is a control flow statement that repeats a block of code as long as a specified condition is true. Instead of writing the same code ten times, you write it once inside a loop and let Java repeat it for you. This saves time, reduces errors, and makes your code easier to read.

The **for loop** is the most common loop when you know exactly how many times you want to repeat. Its header has three parts: initialization (runs once at the start), condition (checked before every iteration), and update (runs after every iteration). Example: `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)` runs the body five times.

The **while loop** first checks the condition, and only if it is true does it execute the body. If the condition is false from the beginning, the body never runs. Use a while loop when you do not know in advance how many iterations are needed, such as reading user input until a sentinel value is entered.

The **do-while loop** is similar to the while loop but it checks the condition *after* executing the body. This guarantees the body runs at least once. It is useful for menu-driven programs where you must show the menu before asking the user to choose.

Two important keywords work inside any loop: `break` immediately exits the loop, and `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one. Nested loops (a loop inside another loop) are allowed and are commonly used for patterns and 2D arrays.

definitions.meaning: A control flow statement that repeatedly executes a block of code while a condition remains true.
One single execution of the loop body.
The part of a for loop that sets the starting value of the loop variable, executed only once.
A boolean expression evaluated before (or after, in do-while) each iteration to decide whether to continue looping.
The part of a for loop that changes the loop variable after each iteration.
A keyword that immediately terminates the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement.
A keyword that skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and moves to the next iteration.
A loop whose condition never becomes false, causing the program to run forever unless interrupted.

points: for loop syntax: for (initialization; condition; update) { body }
while loop syntax: while (condition) { body }
do-while loop syntax: do { body } while (condition); — note the semicolon at the end.
do-while always executes the body at least once, even if the condition is false from the start.
Always make sure the loop variable is updated inside the loop to avoid an infinite loop.
break and continue can be used in all three loop types.
In nested loops, break and continue affect only the innermost loop they are placed in.
Exam tip: Trace through loop iterations manually on paper — identify the value of the loop variable at each step and what gets printed.

lesson.summary: A method in Java is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be called multiple times to avoid code repetition.
shortNotes: A method is defined with a return type, name, and optional parameters inside a class.
The `void` keyword means the method does not return any value.
Methods are called by their name followed by parentheses, e.g., `greet()`.
Parameters allow you to pass data into a method; arguments are the actual values passed.
The `return` statement sends a value back to the caller and exits the method.
Method overloading allows multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists.

detailed.explanation:
A **method** in Java is a block of code grouped under a name. You write it once and call it as many times as needed. This makes your program shorter, easier to read, and easier to fix. Every Java program already uses one method you know — `main`.

A method has five parts: an **access modifier** (like `public`), a **return type** (like `int` or `void`), a **method name**, a **parameter list** inside parentheses, and the **method body** inside curly braces. For example: `public int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`.

**Parameters vs Arguments:** Parameters are the variable names listed in the method definition. Arguments are the actual values you pass when you call the method. In `add(3, 5)`, the numbers 3 and 5 are arguments.

When a method has a non-void return type, it must use the `return` keyword to send a value back to the caller. The type of the returned value must match the declared return type exactly, otherwise the code will not compile.

**Method overloading** means you can have two or more methods with the same name in the same class, as long as their parameter lists are different (different number or types of parameters). Java decides which one to call based on the arguments you provide at the time of the call.

definitions.meaning: A named block of code inside a class that performs a specific task and can be called multiple times.
The data type of the value a method sends back. Use `void` if the method returns nothing.
A variable declared in the method signature that receives a value when the method is called.
The actual value passed to a method when it is called.
The combination of the method name and its parameter list that uniquely identifies a method.
Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class.
The keyword used inside a method to send a value back to the caller and exit the method.

points: A method must be defined inside a class in Java — standalone functions do not exist in Java.
If the return type is not `void`, the method MUST have a `return` statement that returns the correct type.
The `main` method signature `public static void main(String[] args)` must be exact for the JVM to run the program.
Static methods belong to the class and can be called without creating an object — useful for utility/helper methods.
Java passes primitive types by value, meaning changes to parameters inside the method do NOT affect the original variable.
Method overloading is resolved at compile time based on the number and types of arguments.
A method name should start with a lowercase letter and follow camelCase convention, e.g., `calculateArea`.
Exam tip: If a method declares a return type other than void and any code path does not return a value, the code will NOT compile.

Confusing parameters and arguments — parameters are the placeholders in the method definition, while arguments are the actual values passed during the call.
Calling a non-static method without creating an object, or calling a static method on an object instance — always check whether the method is `static` before calling it directly from `main`.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument in Java methods.
questions.answer: A parameter is a variable declared in the method definition that acts as a placeholder for incoming data. An argument is the actual value passed to the method when it is called. questions.explanation: Students often mix these terms. Parameters belong to the method signature; arguments belong to the method call.

questions.prompt: What is method overloading and why is it useful?
questions.answer: Method overloading is the ability to define multiple methods with the same name in the same class, provided their parameter lists differ in number or type of parameters. It is useful because it allows the same operation (like `add`) to work with different data types (int, double) without needing different method names, making the code more readable and intuitive.
questions.explanation: Overloading improves code readability and follows the principle of using one logical name for the same kind of operation regardless of data type.

Let us quickly recap what we learned today about methods in Java.

Use the return keyword to send a value back. Arguments are the real values you pass when calling a method.

lesson.summary: An array in Java is a fixed-size, indexed collection of elements of the same data type, stored in contiguous memory locations.
shortNotes: An array stores multiple values of the same type under one variable name.
Array indices start at 0 and end at length-1.
Declare and create: int[] arr = new int[5]; allocates space for 5 integers.
Array elements are accessed using arr[index] syntax.
The length of an array is obtained using arr.length (not a method, no parentheses).
Arrays have a fixed size once created; they cannot grow or shrink dynamically.

detailed.explanation:
An **array** is a data structure that lets you store multiple values of the **same data type** under a single variable name. Instead of declaring five separate variables like `int a1, a2, a3, a4, a5;`, you can simply write `int[] marks = new int[5];`. This makes your code cleaner and easier to manage, especially when dealing with large amounts of data.

In Java, array indices always **start at 0**. So for an array of size 5, valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Accessing `marks[5]` on a size-5 array will cause an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime. Always remember: last valid index = `length - 1`.

You can declare, create, and initialise an array in one line using an **array literal**: `int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88};`. Java automatically sets the size based on the number of values you provide. You can also first declare (`int[] marks;`), then create (`marks = new int[5];`), and then assign values individually.

To process all elements of an array, a `for` loop or an **enhanced for loop** (for-each) is commonly used. The enhanced for loop `for (int m : marks)` reads as "for each integer m in marks" and is cleaner when you only need to read elements. When you need the index (e.g., to modify elements), use the regular `for` loop with `arr.length`.

By default, numeric arrays are initialised to **0**, boolean arrays to **false**, and object arrays to **null**. This is different from local primitive variables, which are not initialised automatically. Understanding default values prevents bugs when you forget to assign a value before using it.

definitions.meaning: A fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory.
The position of an element in an array, starting from 0.
A shorthand way to declare and initialise an array at once, e.g., int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
A runtime error thrown when you try to access an array element using an index that is negative or greater than or equal to the array length.
A property (not a method) that returns the total number of elements in the array.
A simplified for loop syntax (for-each) used to iterate over all elements of an array without using an index variable.

formulas.name: Last Valid Index
formulas.note: Accessing any index beyond this causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

formulas.name: Array Memory Size (approximate)
formulas.note: For int[5], approximately 5 × 4 = 20 bytes are used.

points: Array indices start at 0, not 1 — this is the most common source of off-by-one errors.
Use arr.length (no parentheses) to get the size; arr.length() does not exist and will cause a compile error.
Arrays in Java are objects; they are created on the heap using the new keyword.
Once an array is created with a fixed size, that size cannot be changed.
Default values: int/long/short/byte → 0, double/float → 0.0, boolean → false, String/Object → null.
The enhanced for loop is best for reading; use a regular for loop when you need to modify elements or need the index.
Multidimensional arrays (e.g., int[][] matrix) are arrays of arrays in Java.
Exam tip: If asked about the output of arr[arr.length], remember it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1-2: Class and main method declaration — standard Java entry point.
Line 5: An integer array 'marks' is declared and initialised with 5 values using an array literal. Java sets the size to 5 automatically.
Line 8: marks.length gives the number of elements (5) without parentheses.
Line 11: marks[0] accesses the first element (85); indices start at 0.
Line 12: marks[marks.length - 1] accesses the last element (88) safely, regardless of array size.

Starting the loop index at 1 or going up to i <= arr.length, which causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException because valid indices are 0 to length-1.
Confusing array declaration (int[] arr;) with array creation (arr = new int[5];) — declaring does not allocate memory; you must use 'new' or an array literal before accessing elements.

questions.prompt: What is the index of the first element in a Java array?
questions.explanation: Java arrays are zero-indexed, meaning the first element is always at index 0.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly creates an integer array of size 4 in Java?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax is int[] arr = new int[4]; The square brackets indicate it is an array type, and new int[4] allocates memory for 4 integers.

questions.prompt: What is the default value of elements in an int array when created using new int[5] in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, integer array elements are automatically initialised to 0 when the array is created using the new keyword.

questions.prompt: Which exception is thrown when you access arr[10] on an array of size 5?
questions.explanation: Accessing an index beyond the valid range (0 to length-1) throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime.

questions.prompt: What does arr.length return for: int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};?
questions.explanation: arr.length returns the total number of elements in the array. The array has 5 elements, so arr.length = 5.

questions.prompt: Which loop type is most suitable when you need to modify elements of an array using their index?
options: Regular for loop with index variable
questions.explanation: The regular for loop provides access to the index variable, which is necessary to assign new values to specific positions in the array. The enhanced for loop only gives a copy of the value.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between declaring an array and creating an array in Java.
questions.answer: Declaring an array means specifying the variable name and type, for example int[] arr;. This does not allocate any memory. Creating an array means using the new keyword to allocate memory, for example arr = new int[5];. Only after creation can you store and access elements.
questions.explanation: Declaration tells the compiler the type; creation allocates actual memory on the heap. Forgetting to create (allocate) before using the array results in a NullPointerException.

questions.prompt: What is an enhanced for loop and when should you prefer it over a regular for loop when working with arrays?
questions.answer: An enhanced for loop (for-each) iterates over each element of an array automatically without needing an index variable. You should prefer it when you only need to read elements, as it is cleaner and less error-prone. However, if you need the index to modify elements or access specific positions, use a regular for loop.
questions.explanation: The enhanced for loop simplifies code by removing index management, but it does not provide the index, making it unsuitable when element modification by position is needed.
nums[1] is 6 and nums[3] is 12. Adding them gives 6 + 12 = 18, which is printed as a single integer.

questions.prompt: Write a Java program that declares an integer array of size 5 with values {4, 8, 15, 16, 23}, finds the largest element in the array using a for loop, and prints it.
questions.explanation: We start by assuming the first element (nums[0] = 4) is the largest and store it in max. We then loop from index 1 to nums.length - 1, comparing each element to max. If we find a larger element, we update max. After the loop, max holds the largest value (23), which is printed.

steps.say: Hello everyone! Today we are going to learn about arrays in Java. Imagine you need to store marks for 5 subjects. Would you create 5 separate variables? That sounds tedious, right?
Instead of five separate variables, an array lets you store all five marks under one single name. It is a collection of values of the same type.
All elements must be of the same data type, such as all integers or all doubles. And the size is fixed when you create the array.
Let us see how to declare and create an array in Java. First, we write the data type followed by square brackets, then the variable name.
This only declares the variable. To actually create the array and reserve memory, we use the new keyword with the size in brackets.
Or we can do both on one line. We can also use an array literal to declare and fill values at the same time. Java sets the size automatically.
Now, this is very important. In Java, array indices always start at zero, not one. So the first element is at index zero.
For our marks array of size 5, valid indices are zero to four. The last valid index is always length minus one.
To access an element, write the array name followed by the index in square brackets. For example, marks at index zero gives us 85.
If you try to access index 5 on a size-5 array, Java will throw an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime. Always stay within bounds.
To process all elements, we use a for loop. We start i at zero and go while i is less than the length of the array.
Inside the loop, we use marks of i to access each element. Notice we use marks dot length without any parentheses.
There is also the enhanced for loop, which is cleaner when you only need to read values. It reads as: for each integer m in marks.
Use the enhanced for loop for reading, and the regular for loop when you need the index to modify elements.

write.content:
Read only -> enhanced for loop
Modify -> regular for loop

steps.say: Great work! Let us quickly recap what we learned today about arrays in Java.
An array stores multiple values of the same type under one name, with a fixed size set at creation.
Indices start at zero, and the last valid index is length minus one. Going beyond throws a runtime exception.
Use arr dot length, without parentheses, to get the size. And choose between regular and enhanced for loops based on whether you need the index. Happy coding!

lesson.summary: Strings in Java are objects of the String class that store sequences of characters and provide many built-in methods for text manipulation.
shortNotes: A String in Java is an object, not a primitive type; it is immutable once created.
Strings can be created using double quotes (string literal) or the new keyword.
Common methods include length(), charAt(), substring(), toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), and trim().
The equals() method compares string content; == compares object references.
Strings can be joined (concatenated) using the + operator.
The String class is part of java.lang, so no import is needed.

detailed.explanation:
A **String** in Java is a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotes, like `"Hello"`. Unlike primitive types such as `int` or `char`, a String is an **object** of the built-in `String` class. Because `String` belongs to `java.lang`, you never need to import it — it is always available.

Strings in Java are **immutable**, meaning once a String object is created, its content cannot be changed. When you appear to modify a string (for example, using concatenation), Java actually creates a brand-new String object in memory. This is important to remember for both performance and logic.

You can create a String in two ways: using a **string literal** (`String name = "Alice";`) or using the `new` keyword (`String name = new String("Alice");`). Literals are preferred because Java stores them in a special memory area called the **String Pool**, which saves memory by reusing identical strings.

The `String` class offers many useful **methods**. For example, `length()` returns the number of characters, `charAt(i)` returns the character at index `i` (indexes start at 0), `substring(start, end)` extracts part of the string, `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` change case, `trim()` removes leading and trailing spaces, and `equals()` compares two strings for equal content.

A very common mistake is using `==` to compare strings. The `==` operator checks if two variables point to the **same object in memory**, not whether they contain the same text. Always use `.equals()` or `.equalsIgnoreCase()` when comparing string values.

definitions.meaning: An object of the java.lang.String class that stores an ordered sequence of characters.
Cannot be changed after creation; any operation that looks like a modification actually creates a new String object.
A special memory region in Java where string literals are stored and reused to save memory.
Joining two or more strings together using the + operator.
The position of a character in a string, starting from 0 for the first character.
A String method that compares the actual content of two strings and returns true if they are identical.

points: String index starts at 0, so the last character is at index length()-1.
Always use .equals() for string comparison, never == for content checks.
substring(start, end) includes start but excludes end — it goes up to end-1.
String methods do not modify the original string; they return a new String.
String is final in Java — you cannot extend (subclass) the String class.
Use + or concat() to join strings; + is simpler and more commonly used.
toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() are locale-sensitive; use them carefully in multilingual apps.
contains(), startsWith(), and endsWith() are handy for searching within strings.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1-2: Declare the class and main method — the program entry point.
Line 5: Create a String literal 'Riya' stored in the String Pool.
Line 6: Create a String using 'new' — stored on the heap, not the pool.
Line 9: Use + to concatenate firstName, a space, and lastName into fullName.
Line 10: Print the full name.
Line 13: length() returns total number of characters in fullName (10).
Line 16: charAt(0) returns the character at index 0, which is 'R'.
Line 19: substring(0,4) extracts characters from index 0 to 3 — gives 'Riya'.
Line 22-23: toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() return new strings in changed case.
Line 26-27: trim() removes leading and trailing spaces from 'messy'.

Line 32: 'c' is created with new, so it is a different object; a==c is false.
